10151-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume five of The Great Events by Famous Historians, supervised by Rossiter Johnson, presents world history in the master-words of eminent historians, arranged in order of time with indices, bibliographies, and chronologies. Its contributors include Charles F. Horne, William Stubbs, Guizot, Green, and Lane-Poole.

The volume's narratives span the ninth to eleventh centuries, from the age after Charlemagne through the introduction of Christianity into Russia in 988 to 1015, and Rafn's saga of Eric the Red. Readers get the early Middle Ages told by historians, with Vikings, missionaries, and kings in vivid narrative.
10364-yeast-a-problem:
Charles Kingsley published this novel, first in serial form, as a problem book about faith and modern life. Its hero, Lancelot Smith, is a young man of means who rides, hunts, and drifts, while deeper questions about God, work, and duty press upon him. Kingsley opens with a fox hunt, in sly contrast to the earnest debate to come.

Through friends, lovers, and preachers, Lancelot tests old church ways against new science and social thought. The novel argues that faith must grow, like yeast, through real life and honest doubt. Readers get a lively Victorian novel of ideas, full of country scenes and sharp talk.
10991-dogs-and-all-about-them:
Robert Leighton, assisted by breed authorities, wrote this large guide to dogs, with seventeen full-page plates. Fifty-two chapters move from the general history of the dog through mastiffs, bulldogs, St. Bernards, Newfoundlands, Great Danes, collies, and terriers of many kinds, to toy breeds and practical chapters on management, breeding, ailments, and the law.

Each breed gets history, type, and show notes, with champion dogs named and pictured, such as the smooth St. Bernard Ch. The Viking. Leighton notes, for example, that the Basset-hound waited until 1880 for a Kennel Club class. Dog lovers and show historians will find the book a rich record of Edwardian breeds, standards, and fashions, written before many breeds changed shape.
11254-poetical-works-of-johnson-parnell-:
Edited by George Gilfillan in Edinburgh in 1855, this volume collects the poems of Samuel Johnson, Thomas Parnell, Thomas Gray, and Tobias Smollett, with memoirs, critical dissertations, and explanatory notes. Johnson's section includes London, The Vanity of Human Wishes, prologues spoken by Garrick, and odes on the seasons. Gray's includes the Elegy, the Progress of Poesy, The Bard, and odes on Eton and adversity. Parnell and Smollett complete the set.

Gilfillan's apparatus aims at the general reader, explaining allusions and judging merit without academic jargon. The book preserves four eighteenth-century poets as mid-Victorians read them, together in one binding. For students of the period, it offers both the poems and a contemporary critical frame.
1249-anthem:
Ayn Rand sets a short dystopian tale in a future where the word I has been erased and men speak only as we. Equality 7-2521, a street sweeper, rediscovers electricity, love, and the self in secret. Rand wrote Anthem in the 1930s, as a short parable of the individual against the state.

Rand wrote Anthem as a hymn to the individual mind against the collective, in spare, biblical prose. The novella serves as a brief introduction to her philosophy, and as a warning tale that still sparks fierce debate. The novella's we-language, broken only at the end by I, gives its climax its power.
1250-anthem:
Ayn Rand's short novel is set in a future where the word "I" has been erased and men live only as "we." Equality 7-2521 is a street sweeper with a mind of his own. He finds a hidden tunnel, rediscovers electricity, and flees to the forest, where he reclaims the forbidden word and his own self.

Rand wrote the tale as a hymn to the individual against the collective, in stark, biblical prose. The novel is brief and fierce, and it has become a touchstone for readers who prize self-reliance. It pairs with her later, longer novels as a statement of her creed.
13468-the-new-jerusalem:
G. K. Chesterton walks backwards through history from his garden between the Chilterns and the Thames toward the place from which Christmas came. His New Jerusalem follows the way of cities and the way of the desert. The gates and streets of the city, and the groups who live there, on a Christmas journey to Palestine.

Later chapters take up the shadow of the problem, the battle with the dragon, the endless empire, the meaning of the Crusade, the fall of chivalry, and the problem of Zionism. Chesterton argues that the prophet of the city is not dead even where denied, and that Moslem and Jewish quarrels alike spring from one mysterious moment in its history. Travel, history, and argument blend throughout.
13559-the-backwoods-of-canada-being-lett:
Catharine Parr Traill writes the backwoods of Canada in letters from the wife of an emigrant officer, published in 1836 under the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge. Her letters describe domestic economy in British America, from arrival off Newfoundland and the Gulf of St. Lawrence to forest clearings, stumps, and new homes.

Lost on an ill-defined road, Traill waits while her husband forces his way through tangled underwood along a bank to find a hidden house. Choppers knock at old stumps like carpenters, and a Baltimore oriole defends her nest against a black snake. A curious nest, woven over a forked spray as if sewn with grey thread, shows Traill's eye for natural detail. The book remains a classic of settler life.
13718-manual-of-ship-subsidies-an-histor:
Edwin M. Bacon's 1911 manual gives a historical summary of ship subsidy systems in all nations, defining subsidy as a government grant in aid of a commercial enterprise. In most countries, he notes, the word means a bounty or premium paid to foster national trade, while Britain used it differently.

Bacon surveys premiums on shipbuilding, navigation and trade bounties, fishing bounties, postal subsidies for ocean mails. Naval subventions, and low-interest government loans, country by country, with France, Japan, and China among those covered. The book is a reference work for students of trade policy, laying out how states bought sea power and commerce with public money before the First World War.
14248-homes-and-how-to-make-them:
E. C. Gardner wrote this 1875 guide as a set of letters between an architect and his friends. It aims to give plain, useful hints to people about to build a home. The letters press for better and truer work, not showy fronts. They speak to builders and to dreamers alike, since most people hope one day to build. Good sense, thrift, and honest craft run through the advice.

Much of the talk turns on rooms that must work hard: kitchens, laundries, and stairs. One housewife will not have a cupboard under the sink, since pots shoved in sooty and wet soon turn damp and foul. Gardner shows soapstone tubs, hot and cold water at hand, and a tin hood that draws steam and smoke off the stove. The book still charms as a record of how Victorians thought a sound house should serve daily life.
15041-the-negro-problem:
Seven Black American writers debate the future of their people in this early 1900s collection, with essays by Booker T. Washington, W. E. B. Du Bois, Charles Chesnutt, and Paul Laurence Dunbar among them. Topics run from schooling and voting rights to law, character, and public life. The range of views is the point.

Washington urges work and saving as the road to wealth and leisure, while Du Bois presses the case for a trained leading tenth. Chesnutt takes up disfranchisement, and Dunbar sketches notable Black Americans. Read together, the essays form a landmark debate, still sharp, about freedom, progress, and what full citizenship should mean.
15630-polly-oliver-s-problem:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published this novel in Boston, New York, and Chicago in 1896, with Houghton, Mifflin, illustrated, with a biographical sketch and portrait. Wiggin, born Kate Douglas Smith in Philadelphia, spent her young womanhood in California, but as a very young child moved to Hollis, Maine, where she usually summered. Her earliest memories belong to Hollis, and she draws character and scene largely from that New England neighborhood.

Eighteen chapters follow Polly Oliver from a declaration of independence and forecasting the future through a doctor's prescription, boarders staying while the Olivers go, letters, missionary work, and hard times. Edgar goes to confession, a lady in black appears, and Polly launches her ships. Wiggin writes a warm story of a girl solving a family problem with pluck, humor, and New England common sense.
15837-jerusalem:
A novel from the Swedish of Selma Lagerlof, translated by Velma Swanston Howard, with an introduction by Henry Goddard Leach. Lagerlof, Sweden's Nobel laureate, tells of Dalarna farmers who follow a preacher to the Holy Land. The Ingmarssons open the book, ploughing a summer field in bright morning air. Three books carry the tale from farm to pilgrimage.

At the schoolmaster's, in Zion, and through the wild hunt, Hellgum's new way draws followers. The loss of L'Univers, Hellgum's letter, and the auction lead to the departure of the pilgrims. Gertrude, the dean's widow, and Hok Matts Ericsson share the road. The novel endures as a saga of faith: home left for heaven, at a price paid in full.
16175-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Number fifty-two of The Great Round World, dated November 4, 1897, leads with a sad shipwreck off Cuba. On October 16 the Spanish steamer Triton, carrying soldiers' ammunition, money, and mules for the war in Pinar del Rio, wrecked off that coast on a run from Havana to Bahia Honda. Sailors on the dock had feared for her, since her decks rode only a few feet above the water under her heavy load.

The children's paper retells the wreck in plain, short sentences, turning a distant colonial war into a human story of storm and cargo. Its young readers could follow Cuba week by week without wading through adult newspapers. The issue preserves a schoolroom view of Spain's Cuban troubles in the fall of 1897.
18419-liberalism-and-the-social-problem:
Winston Spencer Churchill, member of Parliament, published this book of speeches and writings with Hodder and Stoughton in London in 1909, in a second edition. Liberalism and the Social Problem gathers Churchill's case for the Liberal government of his day, when he served as a young minister. The book argues that liberalism, rightly understood, must meet the social problem: poverty, unemployment, and the conditions of working life.

Part one records the government: the conciliation of South Africa, the Transvaal and Orange Free State constitutions, liberalism and socialism, imperial preference, and the House of Lords. Part two turns to social organization: the mines eight hours bill, unemployment, the social field, the approaching conflict, the anti-sweating bill, and labour exchanges with unemployment insurance. Readers get Churchill before the wars: a reforming liberal arguing that the state must insure its people against want.
19905-clovers-and-how-to-grow-them:
Thomas Shaw wrote Clovers and How to Grow Them for practical farmers. Each clover variety gets history, character, and range first. Soil adaptation for that variety comes next. Shaw then covers its place in the crop rotation. Preparing the soil, sowing, and pasturing follow in order. Harvesting for hay, securing seed, and renewing the stand complete the course.

Clovers fix nitrogen and feed livestock at once. Shaw, an agriculture professor, made them a system. His orderly chapters turn one crop into farm profit. Period seed practice differs from today's in telling ways. The book preserves varieties farmers once depended on. It remains useful to historians of the legume revolution.
19937-the-departing-soul-s-address-to-th:
The Departing Soul's Address to the Body is a fragment of early English religious poetry. This edition prints it with an English translation. Its editor compares it with the poem called The Grave. Thorpe called The Grave a singularly impressive and almost appalling fragment. Some lines and thoughts are identical between the two poems. Both come from the same school and age of writing. The soul, departing, reproaches the body it leaves.

Soul-and-body debate poems are among England's oldest surviving lyrics. The dead soul lists the body's sins and coming decay. Worms and earth wait in every version of the speech. Scholars use fragments like this to date dialects and verse forms. The translation makes the harsh little poem readable. It is medieval mortality in concentrated form.
20342-grace-harlowe-s-problem:
Grace Harlowe's Problem brings Jessie Graham Flower's schoolgirl heroine to the seaside. Emma Dean drawls her praise of a noble enterprise with dry humor. She calls herself a living witness to the truth of it. Before now, she asks, when has she played in clean sand at all?

Or bathed in the nice green ocean by the shore, she adds. Grace and her friends face a problem that talk alone cannot solve. The series mixes school loyalty, trips, and small moral tests. Readers get Edwardian girlhood at the beach, bright and good-hearted.
20569-dulcibel-a-tale-of-old-salem:
Dulcibel: A Tale of Old Salem, published in 1907, is a historical novel of Puritan Massachusetts. On a sunny autumn afternoon nearly two hundred years before, a young man walks a newly opened road. The road leads into Salem village, now called Danvers Centre.

Salem in those days still belonged to the Province of Massachusetts Bay. The village roads, meeting houses, and farms stand at the edge of the witchcraft years. Dulcibel's story moves through that stern world of faith and fear. The novel lets readers walk the old roads with the people who feared the devil among them.
20722-a-little-girl-in-old-salem:
Published in 1908, Amanda M. Douglas's novel places a young girl in old Salem, the historic port town in Massachusetts. One early scene shows Chilian at the breakfast table, book in hand, eating slowly while he thinks. Small, quiet moments like that set the tone for a story built on home life.

Douglas uses the girl's daily world to bring a famed old town within reach of young readers. Meals, visits, talk, and town customs carry most of the interest. Readers get a gentle picture of an earlier America, told at a child's pace and in plain, warm language.
21334-the-beaux-stratagem:
George Farquhar wrote this comedy near death. His own advertisement says illness stopped him mending faults the reader may find. Actor Mr Wilks's care, he adds, made its stage success. The scene is Lichfield. Two young beaux, short of money, travel the country posing as master and servant to hunt rich wives.

Their stratagem at the inn brings them among country fools, a highwayman landlord, and women cleverer than the hunters expect. Charles Cowden Clarke praised the play as reading as well as it acts, full of life, wit, and sweet temper. First played in 1707, it became Farquhar's most lasting comedy, a late flower of Restoration theatre with a softer heart.
21614-for-the-temple-a-tale-of-the-fall-:
G. A. Henty tells of Jerusalem's fall in For the Temple, a tale of the revolt against Rome. Chapters open on the Lake of Tiberias and a storm on Galilee. John, the young hero, is swept into the rising of his people.

The siege of Jotapata, the fall of the city, and a massacre on the lake follow. John passes among the mountains, into captivity, and at last to Jerusalem itself. Henty shows defenders who were a small, desperate part of the city's crowd. Titus, Josephus, and the storming of the Temple close a tale of civil strife and ruin.
21652-klondike-nuggets-and-how-two-boys-:
E. S. Ellis sends two boys to the goldfields in Klondike Nuggets, published in 1898 with twenty-four pictures. An old Argonaut who crossed the plains in 1849 guides their party's lore. He lost his parents and sister on that trek and never went back east.

Chapters run from Juneau up the Lynn Canal and through Chilkoot Pass. An avalanche, plotters, and Lake Bennett test the boys on the road to Dawson City. Prospecting brings a find, a claim, and a golden harvest at last. Ellis, who wrote the Deerfoot tales, turns the great Klondike rush into a boys' adventure within a year of the event.
21868-french-and-oriental-love-in-a-hare:
An uncle's astonishing will drops a young Frenchman into a harem in Mario Uchard's French and Oriental Love in a Harem. This edition was limited to one thousand numbered copies for mature collectors of literary curiosa, with decorations by Paul Avril. The tale unfolds in letters to a friend named Louis. The writer swears he is neither dead, ruined, a pirate, nor a monk, as his four months' silence might suggest.

His uncle, called the Corsair, was a Marseilles orphan who raised his baby sister and amassed a strange fortune. The will surpasses, the nephew says, any feat a notary's pen ever managed. What follows mixes French wit with oriental romance. The book is a period piece of Gallic adventure, frank for its day.
23232-the-servant-problem:
Robert J. Young's The Servant Problem is a work of science fiction built around a strange device. In a bowl sits an object that looks, startlingly, like a goldfish, though it is nothing of the sort. Each time Francis adds another attachment, the thing grows brighter.

Soon its glow is so fierce that Francis must wear cobalt-blue goggles to look at it. Young plays a domestic-sounding title against a scene of invention running hot. Readers get a tale where a household problem meets an experiment whose light, and whose risks, keep rising with every new part fitted.
24262-antinous-a-poem:
Fernando Pessoa wrote this poem, published in Lisbon by Monteiro and Company in 1918. It opens with rain falling right into Hadrian's soul, while the boy Antinous lies dead on a low couch, the shadowy light of death's eclipse shed over him. Outside, day seems night, and the rain falls as if nature herself recoiled at the killing.

Hadrian remembers hands that once clasped his warm hands, hair, eyes, lips, and a body like a god dawning into humanity, all now cold and still. The emperor collapses beside the couch, his grief like a rage, knowing the gods take back the life they gave and spoil the beauty they made. Readers get a brief, intense elegy on love, loss, and empire.
24290-problem:
Alan E. Nourse wrote this comic science fiction story about a public-relations problem with teeth. Pete Greenwood gets a letter, too early for the regular mail, bearing a New Philly photocancel and a dreadful premonition. Tommy Heinz writes from the East in haste. A Grdznth problem is becoming a Problem. He needs a salesman skilled with iceboxes to get gators out of his hair fast. The math boys are hot on it, and citizens are not.

Pete sighs and boards the Eastbound Rocketjet. He watches a huge reptilian head materialize in the aisle, followed by a scaly green body with razor talons and a whiplash tail tipped with a needle. The creature pirouettes and settles like an eight-foot balloon. Readers get a hilarious tale of aliens loose and PR in over its head.
24682-quilts-their-story-and-how-to-make:
Marie D. Webster wrote this book on quilts, their story and how to make them, published at Garden City, New York, in 1916 with illustrations. A frontispiece shows an Indiana Wreath quilt made in 1858, in red, green, yellow, and pink. Webster's introduction leads into chapters on patchwork in antiquity and after.

Later chapters trace quilt patterns, materials, and methods, with guidance for makers. Webster, herself a designer, writes with knowledge and love for an American craft. Quilters today still prize her book as a classic, and readers interested in folk art will enjoy its history and its handsome pictures.
28260-captain-sword-and-captain-pen-a-po:
Leigh Hunt wrote Captain Sword and Captain Pen in 1835 as a poem against war, with remarks on war and military statesmen. Hunt, dedicating the book to Lord Brougham, praises him as promoter of education, expediter of justice, liberator from slavery, and denouncer of war. The poem's measure, four accents to a verse, follows the style of Christabel.

Captain Sword stands for glory by violence, Captain Pen for glory by peaceful means, in Milton's words quoted on the title page. Hunt wrote from a sense of duty in a public crisis, hoping many small voices might hasten reason and beneficence. The poem remains a strong early peace plea in verse.
2829-fanny-and-the-servant-problem:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote Fanny and the Servant Problem as a four-act comedy about a household that cannot keep its staff. Fanny Wetherell, her husband Vernon, and their circle argue over butlers, housekeepers, and maids while family pride and old titles complicate every hiring. The title names the running joke, since the servants cause less trouble than the people who employ them.

Jerome builds the comedy from crossed conversations, social rank, and the gap between what the family claims and what it can manage. Lord Bantock's family history, including the clever woman who won its title, becomes part of the teasing. The play still amuses as a light attack on Edwardian snobbery and the myth of the well-run house.
28437-it-s-a-small-solar-system:
Allan Howard's short science-fiction vignette It's a Small Solar System looks back to the days when readers spent more time on Barsoom than in Brooklyn. The narrator, once head of Project P-4, recalls a hero of his youth: a writer of Mars stories whom he thought greater than Babe Ruth, Lindbergh, or the President.

Time dimmed that hero's fame, and the first crewed Moon landing seemed to make him obsolete. Then three representatives of Earth walk on Mars, the captain first to touch soil, and the old writer's dreams win a glorious vindication. Howard's story is a fond tribute to pulp imagination meeting real spaceflight.
28686-wild-ducks-how-to-rear-and-shoot-t:
Captain W. Coape Oates's Wild Ducks, published by Longmans, Green and Company of London, New York, and Bombay in 1905, teaches rearing and shooting in four chapters. Photogravure plates from drawings by G. E. Lodge and twelve photographs from life illustrate the work. Oates begins with the first choice any wild-fowl keeper must make: the locality.

Birds do best, he argues, beside a good-sized stretch of water, fed and drained by a stream. Running water brings fresh food after rain, floods back food from the main river, and raises the share of fertile eggs. Shelter in a stackyard or paddock, behind a flood bank or tall hedge, completes the home. Shooting closes the practical guide.
28924-collector-s-item:
Robert F. Young wrote this short science fiction story about a Galactic Historian condensing the histories of ten thousand races into one volume. The task, set by the Galactic Board of Education, has nearly defeated even his renowned abilities, and he has thrown up all five of his hands in despair. At last the manuscript lies finished on his desk, needing only a final reading.

The story's title points to its quiet horror: even the most trivial things can find their way into the weaving of a nest, and the human race is one of them. Young, praised in the magazine's introduction for lyrical intensity, turns here to cool, cosmic analysis. Readers get a short, chilling tale about history, scale, and how small a whole species can look from far away.
28996-miss-grantley-s-girls-and-the-stor:
Thomas Archer wrote this 1886 book about Miss Grantley, a governess, and the girls she teaches, published by Blackie and Son in London. Miss Grantley is about thirty, not a beauty but not plain, superior looking and rather remarkable, though no one can quite say why she draws the eye. She walks well and moves with ease, standing little taller than Marion Cooper, the tallest girl in the first class.

Each day brings a story. Monday brings the silver goblet, Tuesday a baby's hand, and Wednesday a stranger from London. Thursday brings a bookworm, Friday a tale of living and loving, and Saturday Miss Grantley's brother. Archer frames the stories inside school life, with a picture of Antoine discovering a miniature. Readers get a warm Victorian school book, where a governess teaches by tale as much as by lesson.
29212-prehistoric-structures-of-central-:
Martin Ingham Townsend of Troy, New York, delivered this lecture in 1895 on the prehistoric structures of Central America. Europeans after Columbus, he notes, soon met buildings of great magnitude and architectural beauty in the central part of the continent. The question of the lecture is plain: who erected them?

Townsend weighs whether Greek and Roman scholars of antiquity knew about the western continent, whether Phoenicians could have reached it, and what evidence on the continent itself shows about the builders. He also considers the religious belief of the peoples who raised the towers and temples. Readers get a nineteenth-century speculation on American antiquity, earnest and wide-ranging, from before modern archaeology settled many of its questions.
29354-this-one-problem:
M. C. Pease wrote this science fiction story about piracy in the far future. Piracy in the past wears the gaudy colors of romance, the magazine says, and piracy in the present is as tawdry as tabloid headlines. Piracy in the future, vividly told, can be scary stuff. Pease's shortest route between two points may wind the long way around.

Marc Polder, Resident Comptroller of Torran, strolls a dusty street on an asteroid base under a pint-sized moon. Torran, dirty and squalid, houses only the scum of the solar system, though memory may one day make it heroic. Polder enters its restaurant to meet his only aide. Readers get a compact tale where a path of dishonor may turn into the high road to virtue.
29990-satellite-system:
H. B. Fyfe wrote Satellite System for Analog Science Fact and Fiction in October 1960, with pictures by Summers. Its headnote says Fyfe is quite right: there is nothing like a satellite system for a cold storage arrangement, keeping things handy but out of the way. 

A ninety-degree wedge of a cylinder forms his cabin, hardly eight feet high and just over ten feet across the outer arc. Two corners of his hinged three-by-seven bunk had to be beveled to clear the sides. Lockers flatten the arc behind the bunk. Tremont maneuvers into eighteen inches between bunk and a flat surface cutting off the wedge's point, folds the bunk upward, and hooks it fast. A double door in the flat surface reveals a three-foot-square shaft, with light leaking through a partly open hatch above.
30010-trees-are-where-you-find-them:
Arthur Dekker Savage wrote Trees Are Where You Find Them, with pictures by Philip Parsons. Its headnote gives old Doc Yoris's claim: the trees on Mars are few and stunted, there is plenty of gold, of course, but trees can be much more important. The trouble, the narrator says, started at the Ivy, a moving picture house in Cave Junction built like a big quonset. It is the only show in the timber country of southwest Oregon, where old-timers go on Saturday nights before heading for a tavern.

Doc Yoris, there with Lew and Rusty and the narrator, has seen only two or three shows in his life. He comes to Cave Junction only after dark, in dark glasses. When the scientific picture shows men leaving a rocket ship on Mars to look at trees, Doc begins to cackle.
30290-our-homeland-churches-and-how-to-s:
Sidney Heath teaches readers how to study homeland churches in Handbook 55 of the Homeland series, published in London in 1907. Heath, author of Some Dorset Manor Houses, illustrates the book himself with Ethel M. Heath, and photographs support the text under general editors Prescott Row and Arthur Henry Anderson. A front picture shows foundations of a Romano-British church uncovered at Silchester.

The Homeland Association, which encouraged touring in Great Britain, issued the handbook from Bride Lane, Fleet Street, and its editorial note invites suggestions to make future editions more accurate and comprehensive. Readers learn to read a church building itself, from foundations and fabric to fittings and setting, as a record of local history. The book suits walkers and students who want churches as documents, not only as scenery.
30661-pedagogics-as-a-system:
Karl Rosenkranz writes Pedagogics as a System, translated from German by Anna C. Brackett and reprinted from the Journal of Speculative Philosophy, published in St. Louis in 1872. Rosenkranz, doctor of theology and professor of philosophy at Konigsberg, treats education as a system, not a set of tricks.

Transcriber notes keep hyphenated and unhyphenated spellings as they occur, since both forms appear with almost equal frequency and a hyphen may mark emphasis, as in re-formation. The book entered for copyright in 1872 by William T. Harris. It serves teachers and students of education who want a philosophical account of teaching, learning, and formation. The book is slow and careful. It walks a teacher step by step through aims, order, and habit, so the whole art of teaching holds together as one plan.
30795-the-song-of-hiawatha-an-epic-poem:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote this epic poem, held here in the Minnehaha Edition from Donohue in Chicago, with an 1898 copyright. An introductory note says the poem first appeared in 1855, and that Longfellow gathered Native American traditions into one grand poem. Its twenty-two cantos run from The Peace-Pipe and The Four Winds through childhood, fasting, friends, sailing, and fishing to wooing and a wedding feast.

Later cantos follow the Son of the Evening Star, blessing the cornfields, picture-writing, lamentation, Pau-puk-Keewis, the death of Kwasind, ghosts, famine, the white man's foot, and Hiawatha's departure. Longfellow's steady, musical rhythm made the poem a household favorite in its day. Modern readers should note that its Indian tales are Longfellow's literary retelling, not a tribal record, and enjoy it as a classic American poem.
31686-collector-s-item:
Evelyn E. Smith's Collector's Item, produced from Galaxy Science Fiction of December 1954 and illustrated by EMSH, opens on Venus with a lizard-man bearing off the shrieking Miss Anspacher in his scaly arms. Professor Carl Bernardi gazes after them and wonders whether the creature plans to eat her or court her, and whether, in the latter case, they should interfere at all.

His wife cries out that he must rescue her at once, and Bernardi gives her a grin he knows will irritate her before agreeing. A sidenote warns that Venusian heat does not excuse bad manners, though anyone abducted, marooned, tricked, and kept from tea might well crack. Smith's comedy keeps its manners even on Venus.
32099-the-titanic-disaster-poem:
J. H. McKenzie's Titanic Disaster Poem, published at Guthrie, Oklahoma, in May 1912, is a verse account of the sinking written within weeks of the event. Its title page states the facts plainly: the event took place on the night of April 14, 1912, on the Titanic's first Atlantic voyage to New York. McKenzie's poem retells the disaster in rhymed stanzas for a popular audience.

The opening stanzas picture the maiden ship on a cold, dark Atlantic, valued at ten million and grandest ever to roam the seas. She bids farewell to England in robes of white and glides westward, until a watchman views a monster a mile away. Warned by a German vessel of an iceberg ahead, the great ship steams on toward the sea monster seamen dread. Readers get a contemporary ballad of the Titanic, earnest, topical, and unpolished.
32528-the-lusiad-or-the-discovery-of-ind:
Luis de Camoëns's epic The Lusiad, translated from Portuguese by William Julius Mickle with a life of the poet, tells the discovery of India in heroic verse. This fifth edition, revised by E. Richmond Hodges and published in London in 1877, carries an original dedication of 1776 to the Duke of Buccleuch. Mickle explains that his father served for years as a clergyman under the duke's family, earning marks of favour from the late duke and the Earl of Dalkeith.

A quotation from Hallam in the front matter praises the poem as a mirror of a heart full of love, courage, generosity, and patriotism. The epic follows Portuguese voyagers, gods, storms, and new shores, turning sea history into national myth. Readers get a classic of European epic poetry in a readable, well-annotated English translation.
32552-american-languages-and-why-we-shou:
Daniel G. Brinton's American Languages, and Why We Should Study Them, delivered before the Pennsylvania Historical Society on March 9, 1885, pleads for a neglected branch of learning. Brinton argues that American aboriginal languages deserve study, even though they survive mainly in thousands of geographical names across the land.

Connecticut alone holds over six hundred such names, and Pennsylvania holds even more. Brinton urges scholars to preserve their correct forms and meanings, and to draw on native tongues for new place names instead of repeating Athens, Rome, Troy, and Washington for place after place.
32840-one-of-them:
Charles James Lever's two-volume novel, illustrated by Phiz and published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1902, opens with an apology for its title. Lever offers an Eastern parable of a poor man puzzling how to eke out a livelihood, then lets the story itself justify the name. The dedication, from Spezia, goes to James Whiteside, a friend from his own country.

Volume one follows a piazza after sunset, the Villa Caprini, travelling acquaintances, and Mrs. Penthony Morris at her writing-table. Volume two moves from a lone villa on the Campagna to Baden, Bregenz, and Rome. Along the way come the member for Inchabogue, the O'Shea at his lodgings, old letters, and a lecturer named Quackinboss. The novel closes with three meeting again.
3291-john-marshall-and-the-constitution-:
Edward S Corwin writes this life of John Marshall and his Court for the Chronicles of America series. Volume sixteen of the series, published by Yale University Press, takes the Supreme Court as its subject and Marshall as its maker. The chief justice who shaped American law from 1801 to 1835 stands at the center of every chapter.

Corwin traces how Marshall turned a weak bench into a co-equal power: judicial review, federal supremacy, and the contract clause among his tools. The Constitution as a story, not a text alone: that is Corwin's method, and Marshall gives it a hero. Marshall's long tenure becomes, in Corwin's telling, the biography of an institution finding its voice.
33194-the-warfare-of-the-soul-practical-:
Shirley C. Hughson's studies treat temptation as a real warfare of the soul, fought day by day in ordinary life. A priest of the Order of the Holy Cross, Hughson draws on masters of the spiritual life through the ages, offering their counsel in plain, practical form. Published in 1910, with a preface by Alfred G. Mortimer, the book aims to help readers know God better, love him more truly, and serve him more faithfully.

The studies move through the ways temptation comes, grows, and can be met, always with an eye to habit and prayer rather than theory alone. Hughson's tone is gentle and direct, suited to private reading and quiet thought. For readers who want old wisdom set out in clear modern English, the volume remains a useful guide to the inner life.
33323-small-gardens-and-how-to-make-the-:
Violet Purton Biddle's guide shows how to make the most of small gardens, with practical advice on planting, dividing, cuttings, seeds, and layers. The book speaks to town gardeners with little ground, teaching them to choose plants that earn their place, to use every sunny corner, and to keep a garden tidy through the seasons. Its tone is plain and encouraging, suited to beginners.

Beyond its how-to chapters, the guide reflects a time when seed lists and bulb sellers filled the back pages, and a good garden was a point of pride. Biddle's advice on bulbs, flowers, and vegetables still reads well today. For readers with a small plot and big hopes, it is a handy, old-fashioned manual, full of sense and thrift.
33370-soap-bubbles-and-the-forces-which-:
C. V. Boys's Soap-Bubbles and the Forces Which Mould Them gathers three lectures given at the London Institution in late 1889 and early 1890, before a juvenile audience. Boys shows how bubbles form, join, and burst, and how a fountain breaks into drops under musical sound, with experiments that make physics visible. His lectures turn a child's toy into a window on surface tension and force.

The book's charm lies in its clear, playful experiments, each explained in plain language for young listeners. Boys, a fellow of the Royal Society, writes with a teacher's delight in wonder. For readers of popular science, it remains a classic: a short, joyful introduction to the hidden forces that shape a bubble's brief, bright life.
33430-mosada-a-dramatic-poem:
W. B. Yeats's Mosada, a dramatic poem reprinted from the Dublin University Review and printed in Dublin in 1886, is an early work by the poet who would become Ireland's voice. With a frontispiece portrait of the author by J. B. Yeats, the poem presents a dramatic tale in verse, shaped by the young Yeats's love of legend, mood, and musical speech.

The poem suits readers who trace Yeats from his beginnings, before his later, greater plays and lyrics. Its verse moves with a dreamlike grace, and its story, told through speakers rather than a narrator, gives it a stage-like feel. For students of Irish literature, Mosada is a precious early sign of a master in the making.
34050-konrad-wallenrod-an-historical-poe:
Adam Mickiewicz wrote this historical poem, translated from the Polish into English verse by Miss Maude Ashurst Biggs and published in London in 1882 by Trubner and Company. Parts run from the Election through the Festival and War to the Parting, with notes and prefaces by author and translator. A Machiavelli epigraph on fighting as fox and lion opens the book.

Mickiewicz's preface tells how the Lithuanian nation, formed from Litwini, Prussian, and Leti tribes in a small, infertile land, rose in the thirteenth century against neighbors' incursions. The poem follows Konrad Wallenrod among Teutonic knights, Poland, Novgorod, and the Volga lands. It remains a classic of Polish romantic poetry.
34125-the-sarva-darsana-samgraha-or-revi:
Madhava Acharya's Sarva-Darsana-Samgraha, here in the 1882 London translation by E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough, reviews the systems of Hindu thought one by one. Sixteen chapters take up rival schools, from the Charvaka and Buddhist systems to the Jaina, Nyaya, Sankhya, Yoga, and Vedanta.

Each chapter sets out a school's claims about the world, knowledge, and the path to freedom, in the school's own terms. The book suits readers who want a clear map of old Indian debate, drawn from a Sanskrit work that was long scarce even in India. Cowell's preface recalls the stir among learned Hindus at Calcutta when the Sanskrit text first appeared in print.
3426-on-books-and-the-housing-of-them:
This essay treats a book as a thing with a body and a soul, and asks how its body should be made and kept. It moves through jewelled bindings, illuminated pages, and the small portrait art once called miniature work, then turns to the modern age of cheap printing and boundless demand. The author warns that noble works should not appear in mean, worthless forms.

Cheapness, the essay argues, needs a limit set by fitness: a book's dress should suit its worth. Readers who love libraries, binding, and the craft of printing will find a thoughtful case for care in how books are produced and shelved. The piece also reflects an older book world, when a fine binding was part of reading itself.
4616-lessons-in-life-for-all-who-will-re:
T. S. Arthur published Lessons in Life, for All Who Will Read Them, at Philadelphia in 1851, opening with the truism that we are never too old to learn. At every stage of existence, he says, we are learners. If we con well the lessons written in the great Book of Human Life we will be wiser and happier. The stories here were written to make that study easier.

Contents include The Right of Way, Coals of Fire, A New Pleasure, and The Daughter-in-Law. They go on to Smith and Jones, He Must Have Meant Me, For the Fun of It, Forgive and Forget, and Paying the Minister. Had I Been Consulted, The Mistakes of a Rising Family, and The Means of Enjoyment close the set. Stories for Parents was to follow in the Library for the Household. Readers get short moral tales for family use.
5137-fair-em:
Fair Em is an Elizabethan comedy printed under Shakespeare's name, though scholars now count it apocryphal rather than his work. Its plot joins two worlds: William the Conqueror, courting in disguise. Em, the miller's daughter of Manchester, tests her plain sense and loyalty against rival suitors, Danish princes, and court intrigue.

The play moves between Windsor, Manchester, and the Danish court, mixing romance, disguise, and clowning. Readers curious about the plays once attributed to Shakespeare will find a lively, if uneven. Comedy that shows what popular Elizabethan theatre offered its audiences beyond the great names.
5175-pearl-maiden-a-tale-of-the-fall-of-:
H. Rider Haggard's Pearl-Maiden, first published in 1901, is set in Judaea at the time of Jerusalem's fall. It opens in the prison at Caesarea and follows Miriam, born in troubled times, enthroned among the Essenes, and caught between Caleb and the Roman Marcus as war closes around the city.

Chapters move from the grain store and the Sanhedrim to the Gate of Nicanor and the death struggle for Jerusalem, with a ring, a necklace, and a letter carrying the plot's secrets. Haggard mixes romance with biblical history, and the novel offers a dramatic, old-fashioned retelling of a famous catastrophe through one woman's life.
6442-bitter-sweet-a-poem:
J. G. Holland builds Bitter Sweet as a poem in movements, each stating and illustrating one question. A prelude and first movement state and argue the question in talk. A first episode illustrates it by nature, and a second movement tells it by experience. A second episode illustrates it by story, a third movement works it out in drama, and an envoy closes. The picture opens on winter's wild birthnight, wind moaning in the fretful east.

Sleet sifts onto huddled leaves and pins them to earth, while a roofless bullock hugs a sheltering stack with dumb endurance. A mid passage turns darker and stranger: the milk haired heifer's life must pass to fill our own, as grass passed to feed her. From lowly woe springs lordly joy, Holland writes, and life's cup passes hand to hand up being's gradation. The poem argues that loss feeds life.
7184-a-heart-song-of-to-day-disturbed-by:
Annie G. Savigny's novel opens with a pretty woman laying a plot and hiring a gardener, and its chapter titles keep that game of masks and motives going. Madame shuffles the cards, Vaura moves through a medley, and Lionel Trevalyon enters a story of love and love-making where velvet paws hide claws. Society bouquets, fates spinning black thread, and flights from earth to earth mark the turns.

Savigny writes a society tale in which talk, scheme, and feeling pull against each other, and the heroine's heart-song is disturbed by the unruly member of the title. The long chapter list promises intrigue, romance, and sharp social comedy in equal share. Readers follow a world where a glance can be a move in a larger game.
7804-expressive-voice-culture-including-:
Jessie Eldridge Southwick, teacher at Emerson College of Oratory, sets out the Emerson system in Expressive Voice Culture. The system treats voice as a natural reporter of the person, always tending to express a thought or feeling in fitting tone. The book links technique to expression throughout.

Southwick warns she offers one person's contribution, not a full science. Yet her first chapter grounds voice work in meaning: the ring of true culture lies in perfect modulation of tone and movement. Speakers, teachers, and readers aloud will find plain methods for making voice match thought.
8146-victor-roy-a-masonic-poem:
Harriett Annie Wilkins wrote Victor Roy as a Masonic poem, dedicated by permission to Daniel Spry, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Canada. Her preface explains that an anecdote in The Craftsman gave rise to the poem, and that it aims neither at Alpine heights of imagination nor at undiscovered treasures of thought. It is a very simple story, told in very simple words, about lives like those around us, sorrows daily borne, and faith that gives strength to suffering humanity.

The poem's Masonic character lies in its moral: brotherhood, endurance, and trust in dark times. Wilkins writes plainly, for readers rather than critics, and her verses suit reading aloud in a lodge or at home. As Canadian verse of its period, it preserves a modest, sincere voice, and a glimpse of Masonic ideals in poetry.
8536-philip-gilbert-hamerton-an-autobiog:
Philip Gilbert Hamerton tells his own life from 1834 to 1858 in this autobiography, and his wife continues it as a memoir from 1858 to 1894. Hamerton opens on intellectual living. It is not so much an accomplishment as a state of mind, seeking earnestly for the highest and purest truth, even while blundering for want of perfect wisdom and clear light.

Hamerton, an art critic and writer on French life, lived between England and France, and the double narrative follows his formation and his career. Readers get a Victorian life in art and letters, told first by the man himself, then by the woman who knew him best. The volume suits readers of art criticism and of Victorian biography.
8683-the-columbiad-a-poem:
Joel Barlow published The Columbiad in 1809 as an epic poem on Columbus and the founding of America, prefaced by careful remarks on his design. Barlow admits the difficulty of fitting so vast and recent a subject to classical epic form, and of making it both poetical and persuasive. An Italian epigraph from Tasso's Jerusalem Delivered sets Columbus beside Hercules and Bacchus, as a hero whose fame will outlast empires.

The poem follows Columbus's voyage and, in prophetic vision, the rise of the American republic, its institutions, and its future glory. Barlow, diplomat and poet, wrote as a convinced republican, and the epic doubles as political argument in verse. Modern readers may find its optimism and its rhetoric dated, but it remains the most ambitious American epic of its generation, and a key text for the early republic's self-image.
9047-the-banks-of-wye-a-poem:
Robert Bloomfield wrote this poem in four books after a summer trip down the River Wye in 1807 with friends from Gloucestershire. The poem, printed in 1811, follows the party through South Wales, noting river scenes, hills, and the people met on the way. Bloomfield dedicates it to the friends who shared the jaunt.

The verse is gentle and observant, praising the Wye's beauty in plain, musical lines rather than grand rhetoric. It belongs to the age of the picturesque tour, when travelers sought wild scenery with a sketchbook in hand. Modern readers can still enjoy it as a leisurely river journey in verse.
9092-the-farmer-s-boy-a-rural-poem:
Robert Bloomfield's rural poem made him famous, and this third edition shows its early success. The Farmer's Boy follows a shepherd's boy through the seasons, at work with flocks, fields, and country folk. Bloomfield, a working man, wrote from life, not from books. A sonnet by a young lady friend fronts the volume.

The poem praises honest labor, the turn of the year, and the quiet pride of farm life. Its plain verse won readers who seldom read poetry at all. Bloomfield's boy remains a touching figure, and the poem a landmark of English pastoral verse.
9985-pocahontas-a-poem:
Virginia Carter Castleman's narrative poem tells the story of Pocahontas in eight parts, opening with the little princess of her people. Castleman dedicates the poem to Virginia, the mother state, laying one leaf upon its wreath of fame.

The poem follows Pocahontas from childhood among her people through her meeting with the English settlers and the choices that made her famous in two worlds. Castleman writes in a descriptive, patriotic manner suited to school and home reading. Readers get the familiar legend retold as verse, with sympathy for its heroine.
a-heart-song-of-to-day-disturbed-by-fire:
Mrs. Annie G. Savigny signed A Heart-Song of To-Day as a society novel, and its chapter titles promise plots laid by pretty women, cards shuffled by a Madame, and hearts stirred in drawing rooms. The story moves among Vaura, Lionel Trevalyon, and their fashionable circle, where calls, balls, and confidences carry the action forward.

Madame works her schemes through gardeners, letters, and careful talk, while younger characters fall in and out of love under her eye. Chapters lift veils, take the season's mood on the wing, and return to earth with proposals and reversals. The result is a period piece of manners and intrigue, written for readers who liked their romance dressed in satin and spite.
anthem:
Ayn Rand's novella opens with a confession: it is a sin, the narrator says, to write words no others are meant to see. He lives in a future city where men speak of themselves only as 'we,' and the Council of Vocations assigns every person his life's work. Alone in a tunnel by candlelight, he writes his secret journal.

Twelve short parts trace his forbidden experiments with a strange power he finds in a forgotten tunnel, his love for a woman he names to himself, and his flight beyond the city. In the wild he finds an old house and its books. There he recovers a word his world had banned: I.
bitter-sweet-a-poem:
Bitter-Sweet, a poem by J G Holland, is a philosophical poem built like a symphony. Holland's contents divide it into movements. A prelude and a first movement, marked colloquial, state and argue the question. Episodes illustrate it by nature and by story. A second movement is narrative, a third dramatic. The denouement and an envoy close the design. Persons are listed like a cast.

The poem opens on winter's wild birthnight, with wind sighing through mountain gorges and pines. Holland, a bestselling poet and editor, asks why life mixes its gifts with pain. The question is argued, sung, and storied in turn. Bitter-Sweet was among the most read American poems of its century. Families kept it beside the Bible and read the movements aloud. Its symphony structure was the ambition of the age: to make a poem carry what an orchestra carries, argument included.
britannica-1911-archean-system:
Archean system is a geological term for the oldest rocks. The name derives from a Greek word for beginning. These rocks lie below the lowest fossil-bearing strata. Cambrian rocks with Olenellus fauna mark that boundary. A great mass of ancient rock sits beneath them. Stratified, metamorphic, and igneous rocks compose it. Pre-Cambrian is the general term for the whole assemblage. Subdivision is possible in many large tracts.

The Archean proper is the lowermost group. Granitoid, gneissic, and schistose characters prevail there. Its origin is mainly igneous. Sedimentary-looking groups lie above it in sequence. A special name helps where distinction is clear. The long article surveys regions worldwide. Old World and New World examples both appear. Terminology disputes receive careful attention. Geikie's Text Book of Geology anchors references. Chamberlin and Salisbury's Geology also features. John Allen Howe signs the survey.
britannica-1911-baldwin-i-king-of-jerusa:
Baldwin I was prince of Edessa from 1098 to 1100 and then the first king of Jerusalem, reigning to 1118. A brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, he had begun life as a clerk in orders. In 1096 he joined the First Crusade and marched with his brother into Asia Minor.

At Edessa he came first as protector, then, after Thoros was killed, as ruler. Called to Jerusalem on Godfrey's death, he was crowned king on Christmas Day 1100. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his wars in detail. Coast towns such as Arsuf, Caesarea, Acre, Beirut, and Sidon fell to him. Attacks from Egypt were beaten back, and his rule reached toward the Red Sea.
britannica-1911-baldwin-ii-king-of-jerus:
Baldwin II, first known as Baldwin de Burg, was count of Edessa from 1100 to 1118 and then king of Jerusalem until 1131. A son of Count Hugh of Rethel, he was a nephew of Godfrey of Bouillon and of Baldwin I, and he marched with Godfrey on the First Crusade.

Left in charge of Edessa when his cousin took the crown, he raided his Muslim neighbours for years. In 1104 he was beaten and captured, and Tancred held Edessa during his captivity. Freed early in 1108, he had to fight Tancred to regain his county. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his stern, successful rule at that far northern outpost.
britannica-1911-barents-willem:
Willem Barents (died 1597) was a Dutch navigator, born about the middle of the 16th century. In 1594 he left Amsterdam with two ships to seek a north-east passage to eastern Asia. He reached the west coast of Novaya Zemlya and followed it north until ice forced him back near its northern tip.

A second voyage in 1595, with seven ships, came too late to find open water. On the third, his ship was beset after rounding the north of Novaya Zemlya, and the crew wintered in the ice. The party escaped in open boats in June 1597, but Barents died on 30 June. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the later finding of his winter house and relics in 1871, and of part of his journal in 1875.
britannica-1911-bilderdijk-willem:
Willem Bilderdijk (1756–1831) was a Dutch poet, son of an Amsterdam physician. An accident to his foot at age six kept him from active life for ten years. In that idleness he formed habits of hard, close study. His parents backed the House of Orange with ardour. Bilderdijk grew up with strong monarchist and Calvinist views. Da Costa called him anti-revolutionary and anti-liberal on every front he listed.

He took a law doctorate at Leiden in 1782 and practised at The Hague. In 1795 he refused the oath to the new regime and had to leave Holland. Years in Hamburg, London, and Braunschweig followed in exile. The 1911 Britannica entry lists volume after volume of his poems, many written with his second wife. His collected poetical works filled sixteen volumes in the Haarlem edition. His letters and life records fill several more.
britannica-1911-binary-system:
Binary system, in astronomy, names a pair of two stars that revolve around each other. Their mutual attraction, or gravity, holds the pair together on that shared path. The 1911 Britannica entry is a short note of a few lines. It records a change in how astronomers classed such pairs. A line was once drawn between double stars seen to revolve and pairs with no observed motion. That line has been given up since, the entry explains.

The reason is a new general view of double stars. Astronomers now hold that all double stars must really be binary systems. Pairs that show no motion are taken as binaries whose movement has not yet been caught. The entry gives no example stars, periods, or discoverers in its brief space. It sends the reader elsewhere for the working detail of orbits. Its point is the change of definition itself, stated plainly and briefly.
britannica-1911-brummagem:
Brummagem is an old local form of the name Birmingham, and the word carries a sneer. It was first applied to a counterfeit coin made in Birmingham, England, in the 17th century, and later to the plated and imitation articles made there. From coins and cheap metal goods the sense widened until it meant anything cheap, showy or tawdry.

Politics borrowed the insult too. Supporters of the Exclusion Bill in 1680 were particularly called Brummagems, with the meaning of sham Protestants. Their Tory opponents against the Bill were in turn nicknamed Anti-Birminghams or Brummagems, so both sides of that fight wore the label. The short entry holds the word's path from a city's name, through false coin and plated ware, to a standing term for shoddy show and sham religion.
britannica-1911-carboniferous-system:
The Carboniferous system is a great series of rocks in geology. It lies above the Devonian and below the Permian. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the system. Its strata include volcanic rocks as well as layered ones. W. D. Conybeare first applied the name in 1821. He used it for the coal-bearing strata of England and Wales. The grits and limestones beneath them were included.

The name rests on the coal seams in the system. Yet coal forms only a small part of its total thickness. The rocks include marine limestones, shales and sandstones. Fresh-water and estuarine beds also occur in the series. Oil-bearing rocks, gypsum and salt appear among them. The article notes the system's blurred edges in many lands. Its rocks merge into the Devonian below without a sharp line. Its fossils likewise merge into the Permian above.
britannica-1911-cochem:
Cochem is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine province on the Mosel, 30 miles west of Coblenz by the railway to Trier. Its people number 3,500 in the entry's count. Above the town the railway enters the longest tunnel in Germany, at two and a half miles. That tunnel and the river valley together fix the town's setting in the account given here.

Romantic situation is the town's chief quality as described, in the deep and winding valley of the Mosel. It sits at the foot of a hill surrounded by a feudal castle dating from 1051. That castle has been restored in its former style, the entry notes in its brief history. A considerable trade in wines is carried on at Cochem, the one industry named for the town.
britannica-1911-emblem:
Emblem, from a Greek word for something put in or inserted, was first used in Greek and Latin for a raised or inlaid ornament. Such ornaments appeared on vases and other vessels. The word also covered mosaic or tessellated work, patterns built up from small set pieces. The entry is only a few lines long and gives the word's first sense before its modern one.

In English the word is confined to a pictured or symbolic showing of some object. It is used above all when the sign serves as a badge or as a heraldic device, a mark worn or borne to stand for a person, a house, or a body. That narrow modern sense is all the entry claims for present use. A reader gets the path of the word in brief, from a thing laid into a surface to a sign that stands for something beyond itself.
britannica-1911-fulk-king-of-jerusalem:
Fulk, king of Jerusalem (born 1092), was son of Fulk IV, count of Anjou. He became count in 1109 and fought Henry I of England as a steady backer of Louis VI of France. In 1127 Henry won him over by betrothing his daughter Matilda to Fulk son Geoffrey Plantagenet. Fulk had already visited the Holy Land in 1120 and befriended the Templars.

In 1128 Baldwin II of Jerusalem, lacking a male heir, offered Fulk his daughter Melisinda in marriage with the succession. They married in 1129, Acre and Tyre forming her dower, and in 1131 Fulk became king. His reign was quiet and prosperous. Beaten by Zengi near Barin in 1137, he later allied with Damascus against the same foe and took Banias in 1140. He strengthened the south with forts such as Blanche Garde. He died in 1143, leaving Baldwin III and Amalric I to follow him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-apostolica:
Ad Apostolicae Dignitatis Apicem is an apostolic letter against Emperor Frederick II. Pope Innocent IV issued it during the Council of Lyons, on 17 July 1245, in the third year of his pontificate. Innocent first sent three legates to Frederick, chief author of the dissensions tearing those parts, showed the way to peace, and promised his own part in restoring it. Frederick agreed to terms, swore to observe them, and at once violated them.

The letter then lists Frederick's crimes. They include perjury, contempt for papal authority by flouting excommunication, and invasion of pontifical territory. They also include broken peace terms with Gregory, oppression of the church in Sicily, and seizure and killing of bishops bound for a council. Suspicion of heresy, conspiracy with Saracens, and unpaid tribute for Sicily, patrimony of St. Peter. For these crimes Innocent declares Frederick unworthy to rule and frees his subjects from obedience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ad-sanctam-be:
Ad Sanctam Beati Petri Sedem is a letter issued by Alexander VII, dated at Rome on 16 October 1656, in the second year of his pontificate. It confirms the decree of Innocent X condemning five points taken from the Augustinus of Cornelius Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres. Though defined decrees need no backing, Alexander writes because some cast doubt on the definitions or blunt them with false readings, and apostolic authority must promptly remedy the spread of evil.

French bishops had submitted the five points for a clear decision after dispute arose in France. The letter lists them, beginning with claims that some divine precepts are too hard for just men willing to observe them, and that in fallen nature interior grace is not resisted. It declares the points are contained in the Augustinus and condemned in the author's own sense, and it denies that its decision approves other opinions in Jansenius's book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-afflighem:
Afflighem, a Brabant Benedictine abbey near Alost, Belgium, founded by six knights who, abandoning their wild life, resolved to do penance in religion on their former excesses' scene. A church built, they received in 1084 a gift of neighbouring lands from Countess Adela and her sons. The Benedictine rule was adopted, with Wederig as instrument of their conversion, and the abbey later became known for strict observance.

Brabant and Lorraine's dukes and Flanders, Louvain, Brussels, and Bologne's counts patronized and protected it, counting burial in its church a coveted privilege. Several monasteries, Maria-Laach among them, trace their foundation to Afflighem monks. St. Bernard, visiting in 1146, declared he had found angels there, and Our Lady's image is said to have answered his salutation. In 1523 Afflighem joined the Bursfeld Congregation for stricter observance, and in 1569 Mechlin's archbishop became commendatory abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Nidaros, later Trondhjem, owes its Christian beginnings to kings. Norwegians first met the faith on martial expeditions. Haakon the Good, who died in 981, began the work. Converted vikings Olaf Trygvesson, dead in 1002, and Olaf Haraldsson, Saint Olaf, dead in 1030, carried it on, baptized at Andover and Rouen respectively. In 997 Olaf Trygvesson founded Nidaros at the mouth of the River Nid, building a palace and a church there.

From Nidaros he laboured to spread Christianity through Norway, the Orkneys and Shetlands, the Faroes, Iceland, and Greenland. Olaf Haraldsson created an episcopal see at Nidaros and installed the monk Grimkill as bishop. English and German clergy worked beside him. At first Norway's bishops depended on Hamburg-Bremen, then on Lund, primate of Scandinavia. The cathedral stands renewed, though no longer held by the faith that built it. New churches in Saint Olaf's city witness that the Catholic faith lives in Scandinavia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assizes-of-je:
Assizes, in this connection, comes from French asseoir, to seat or place on a seat, hence to put something in its place or determine it. Assise thus came to mean an enactment or statute, and assizes in the plural denotes a court. The Assizes of Jerusalem are the body of laws enacted by Crusaders for the rule of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. They are one collection of legal regulations for tribunals of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem and of Cyprus.

Parallel codes include the Assizes of Antioch for the Latin principality of Antioch and the Assizes of Romania for the Latin realm of Constantinople. It is wrong, the article warns, to ascribe Jerusalem's assizes to Godfrey de Bouillon merely because he was king of Jerusalem and therefore presumed lawgiver. The entry untangles a famous code from its legendary author and places it among Crusader legal collections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethlehem:
Bethlehem, whose Hebrew name means house of bread, receives a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Its Arabic form means house of meat, and some scholars link the name to Lakhmu, a god of Babylonian creation myth, though the entry finds no proof for that guess. Two towns of the name appear in Scripture.

Bethlehem of Judea, five miles south of Jerusalem, outshines its northern namesake, being David's birthplace and, above all, Jesus's. About 10,000 people, almost all Christians, lived there in 1907. Churches, grottoes, and pilgrim sites fill the rest of a place where name, story, and stone meet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-gil-o:
Blessed Gil of Santarem, a Portuguese Dominican, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Vaozela about 1185, son of Coimbra's governor, he died at Santarem in 1265. Boyhood prebends at Braga, Coimbra, Idanha, and Santarem came unasked. But Gil longed not for the Church but for medicine. He studied philosophy and medicine at Coimbra and took a Paris doctorate, working wonderful cures.

A spectre knight twice warned him in his library to change his wicked life. Gil repented, burned his books of magic, and took the Dominican habit at Palencia about 1221. Seven years tormented by a devil's compact ended when the devil surrendered it before Mary's altar. Back in Portugal he became a famed preacher, twice provincial in Spain, and Benedict XIV ratified his cult in 1748.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carem:
Carem was a town of the tribe of Judah. Its name comes from a Hebrew word for vine or vineyard, and it appears in this form only once in the Bible. It occurs only in the Septuagint text of Joshua 15:59, missing with neighboring names from the Vulgate and English versions. Some scholars link it with the Bethacarem of Jeremiah and Esdras, though the link stays open.

Scholars place ancient Carem at 'Ain Karim, a village four miles west of Jerusalem, where village names match the Greek passage. A spring likely took its name from the old town, and the village of about 1,000 people, more than half Muslim, sits on a hill west of the city. A church of the Nativity of John the Baptist stands at its east end. Whether the village is the Baptist's birthplace stays disputed: Fouard doubts it, and Guérin holds to tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-kru:
An entry on Christian Kruik van Adrichem, a Catholic priest and theological writer born at Delft in February 1533. Ordained in 1566, he directed the Convent of Saint Barbara in Delft until the Reformation storm drove him out, and he died at Cologne in June 1585. His works are few but learned, and they made his name among students of the Holy Land.

His Vita Jesu Christi appeared at Antwerp in 1578. His Theatrum Terrae Sanctae et Biblicarum Historiarum at Cologne in 1590 describes Palestine and the antiquities of Jerusalem. It gives a chronology from Adam to the death of John the Apostle in the year 109. The entry rests on Dutch church histories, including Van Heussen and Van Rijn, and a history of Delft of 1729, and it gives the priest his Latin name, Christianus Crucius Adrichomius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elias-of-jeru:
Elias of Jerusalem was a bishop who stood firm for the Council of Chalcedon against Emperor Anastasius I, dying in 518. Anastasius spent most of his reign trying to impose Monophysitism, the teaching that Christ has one nature, on his subjects. At first he sought compromise, but by degrees he went over wholly to the Monophysites, deposing Macedonius of Constantinople in 511 and backing a fierce persecution under Timothy I.

With Flavian of Antioch, Elias was one of only two Catholic bishops who resisted the imperial drive to scrap Chalcedon. When the government called a synod at Sidon in 512 to condemn the council, it was chiefly Elias who blocked that result. An Arab by birth, schooled in an Egyptian monastery and driven out by a Monophysite patriarch in 457, he had come to Palestine and risen to the see of Jerusalem. The entry is a portrait of stubborn orthodoxy under an emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haarlem:
Holland's Diocese of Haarlem was carved from the sprawling medieval see of Utrecht by Paul IV in 1559, with its cathedral at St. Bavo's and the Abbey of Egmond as its revenue. Its first bishop, Nicolas van Nieuwland, held a synod in 1564 and pleaded with the Duke of Alva for leniency, but gout and slowness forced his resignation in 1569.

Godfried van Mierlo, his successor, reconsecrated the pillaged cathedral in 1573. He then watched the sworn pact of equal worship break in the Nona Harlemiana of May 1578, when soldiers attacked the Corpus Christi procession and he fled disguised as a cattle-driver. The entry follows the hidden church under Calvinist rule, the Jansenist split, and the long road back to open Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hesychius-of-:
Hesychius of Jerusalem was a fifth-century presbyter and exegete, a brilliant scholar whose fame long stayed obscure. Almost nothing certain is known of his life, not even the dates of his birth and death. He must not be mixed up with Jerusalem's Bishop Hesychius, who lived in Gregory the Great's day. His writings survive in part lost, in part printed under other authors' names, and in part still buried in manuscript.

Anyone gathering his fragments must return to the manuscripts, since the standard edition throws works of several men named Hesychius together without order. About half that material must be discarded, including a Latin commentary on Leviticus and a set of ascetic maxims that belong to Hesychius of Sinai. The entry sorts genuine homilies and commentaries from false attributions with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-d-okeghe:
Jean d'Okeghem, a composer born about 1430 in East Flanders and dead in 1495, headed the second Netherland school of counterpoint. A choirboy at Antwerp cathedral, he may have studied with Binchois and Dufay, took orders, and in 1453 became chief singer at the court of Charles VII of France.

Okeghem spent most of his life at Tours as treasurer of Saint Martin's by royal appointment, visiting Flanders and Spain at the king's cost. Breaking from strict canon, he let each new voice enter freely at any interval and distance, a principle that reshaped unaccompanied choral writing. His pupils, above all Josquin, carried that freedom across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-latin-kingdom:
The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem rose from the First Crusade in 1099, fell to Saladin in 1187, and lived on around Saint-Jean d'Acre until that city's capture in 1291. For two centuries it served Western Europe as a genuine centre of colonization and, as Christendom's common property, kept an international stamp.

Frenchmen predominated among feudal lords and officials, while Italians held economic sway in the cities. Godfrey of Bouillon, elected Lord of Jerusalem in July 1099, refused the royal crown and died in 1100 after beating Egyptians at Ascalon. His brother Baldwin I, crowned at Bethlehem at Christmas 1100, truly founded the kingdom, seizing Syria's coastal cities with Genoese, Pisan, and Venetian fleets, while Tripoli and Edessa became its fiefs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy-of-je:
The Liturgy of Jerusalem, famed as the Liturgy of St. James, is the old rite of Jerusalem that later spread as the Antiochene use across Syria and Asia Minor. It became the seedbed of the Byzantine rite, though its roots lie in the holy city itself.

No one now holds that James the Less wrote it, yet two local marks betray its birthplace. Prayers invoke the Cross found by Helena at Jerusalem, and the Intercession prays first for Sion, mother of all churches. Cyril's lectures at the Holy Sepulchre around 347 confirm the same rite in use there, tying text to place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manahem:
Manahem was king over Israel for ten years, dated from 743 B.C. by Kautzsch and 745 to 736 by Schrader. Second Kings 15:13-22 tells his short reign in brief. He was called son of Gadi, perhaps of the tribe of Gad. Josephus calls him a general of Israel's army.

When Shallum murdered Zacharias at Samaria and seized the throne, Manahem refused the usurper. He marched from Tirzah, besieged Samaria, took it, killed Shallum, and took the crown himself. He then crushed Thapsa with savage cruelty. His reign matters because Assyria first entered Israel under him. Phul, king of Assyria, now read as Tiglath-Pileser III, came into the land. Manahem paid him a thousand talents of silver, wrung from the wealthy at fifty shekels each, some 60,000 rich men in all. He seems to have died a natural death, and his son Pekahiah followed him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-of-coc:
Martin of Cochem was a celebrated German theologian, preacher, and ascetic writer, born at Cochem on the Moselle in 1630 and dead at Waghausel in 1712. From a family devoted to the faith, he joined the Capuchin novitiate young and stood out for fervour and fidelity to rule. After priesthood he taught theology creditably for several years.

His fame came elsewhere: when plague struck the Rhenish country in 1666, closing novitiates and houses of study, Father Martin turned to popular preaching and religious writing. Through Trier and Ingelheim archdioceses, which he traversed thoroughly, he preached missions and wrote devotional works for ordinary people. His writings, widely reprinted, aimed at renewing faith after Thirty Years War ruin. He laboured with great energy to bring these undertakings to success, and his works long shaped German Catholic piety. He died in the Waghausel convent in 1712.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-st-l:
The Order of Saint Lazarus of Jerusalem began as a leper hospital of the crusader kingdom in the twelfth century. Earlier Eastern leper houses followed Basil's rule, but Jerusalem's house took Augustine's hospital rule, and its claim to remote antiquity as the oldest order is apocryphal.

Unlike Saint John's passing guests, Saint Lazarus's lepers lived in perpetual seclusion as brothers and sisters under a common rule, and some houses even chose a leper as master. The entry follows the order from Jerusalem through Acre, France, and Savoy into its modern hospitaller and chivalric forms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salem:
Salem, also called Salmansweiler or Solomon's Villa, is a Cistercian abbey near Heiligenberg Castle, about ten miles from Constance in Baden. Founded in 1136 by Gunthram of Adelsreute under Innocent II and Emperor Lothair II, it took its second name from the likeness of its first buildings to Solomon's Temple. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a house that grew rich and famous.

Blessed Frowin, once Bernard's travelling companion and interpreter, became first abbot, and under him and his successors the abbey prospered. Great buildings in three squares and a splendid church rose between 1182 and 1311, and Salem became noted for learning and wealth. The entry clears up a common error, showing Salem was not founded from Bellevaux, whatever the confusion over Frowin's earlier home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santarem:
Santarém, a prelature nullius created in 1903 in the province of Belém do Pará, counts a Catholic population of 200,000. Its bishop, Armando Bahlmann, titular bishop of Argos, was born in 1862, appointed in 1907, and consecrated in 1908. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes an Amazon river town and its missions.

The bishop lives at Santarém in Pará state, made a city in 1848 and beautifully placed on the northern bank of the Tapajós river, with 28,000 people. Four parishes divide the city: Santarém, Alter do Chão, Boim, and Villa Franca. Franciscan friars, based at their Santarém monastery, run the prelature's missions, while state funds support a school of over 200 pupils alongside colleges for boys and girls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sem-shem:
Sem, called Shem in the Authorized Version, was a son of Noah and, by one reckoning, the eldest. This short biblical entry follows his life and line from Genesis. He lived six hundred years. One incident shows his filial reverence, when he helped cover his father's nakedness, and his reward was a blessing of great weight.

Noah's words, blessed be Yahweh, the God of Sem, mark Sem in a special way as the bearer of the messianic promises. The entry then runs through the Semitic nations listed in Genesis, whose homes spread over the central known world. It resumes the genealogy through Arphaxad, direct ancestor of Abraham, David, and Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sichem:
Sichem, called Shechem in the Authorized Version, was an Israelite city in the tribe of Ephraim and the first capital of the Kingdom of Israel. Its place is fixed by the Bible north of Bethel and Silo, on the high road from Jerusalem to the northern districts, in the hill country of Ephraim below Mount Gerizim. Josephus puts it between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, and the Madaba map agrees, so the entry identifies it with Nablus, the Neapolis of early Christian times.

The name, from a Hebrew word for shoulder or saddle, may reflect the shape of the ground. A few doubt the city existed in Abraham's day, but none doubt it in Jacob's, and it appears in the Amarna letters and in an Egyptian traveler's account. The entry then follows Sichem through patriarchal story, the division of the kingdom, Samaritan history, and later Christian and Muslim centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alexander-:
St. Alexander died in chains after cruel torments in the persecution of Decius, having served first as bishop of Cappadocia and then as coadjutor at Jerusalem. This entry explains the unusual arrangement: imprisoned for his faith under Alexander Severus, he was freed, came to Jerusalem. And was pressed by its bishop, then 116 years old, to stay and help govern the see, with the consent of all Palestine's bishops.

Alexander famously allowed Origen, still only a layman, to preach in the churches, and when challenged, defended himself with examples of similar permissions granted elsewhere, even to the young Origen. Butler notes the two men had studied together at Alexandria's great Christian school, and the entry follows Alexander on to his martyrdom under Decius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyril-of-j:
Jerusalem's fourth-century bishop Cyril is remembered above all for the teaching talks he gave to people preparing for baptism, and this entry follows both those talks and the stormy career behind them. Born about 315, he rose to the see of Jerusalem and kept it through repeated clashes over doctrine and church rank, dying probably in 386. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 pieces his life together from Jerome, Rufinus, and fifth-century church historians.

At its centre stand the Catecheses, delivered around 347, which lay out Christian belief for newcomers in plain, ordered lessons. Around them the entry traces his long quarrel with Acacius of Caesarea over precedence, his spells of exile, and the shifting charges about his orthodoxy. Readers meet a bishop caught between rival church parties, whose teaching outlasted the controversies that dogged his working life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ephraem:
