Ephraem of Nisibis, who died in June 373, stands among the Syriac church's greatest writers, though much of his work survives only in translation. Born at Nisibis early in the fourth century to a pagan priest of the goddess Abnil, he was taught by Bishop James and baptized at eighteen or twenty-eight. He helped renew the city's moral life through Persian sieges in 338, 346, and 350. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows him from Nisibis into a vast literary afterlife.

One biographer tells how his curse from the walls sent flies and mosquitoes against Sapor II's army. After Julian's disastrous campaign and Jovian's surrender of Nisibis, Ephraem's writings spread in Greek, Armenian, Arabic, Ethiopian, Slavonic, and Latin versions. Many originals perished or lie unfound, and liturgical use added interpolations. The entry maps a writer preserved by translators.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temple-of-jer:
Temple comes from Latin templum, an uncovered place affording a view, and a place sacred to Divinity. Jerusalem's sanctuary bore the Hebrew name Bet Yehovah, house of Jehovah. It held two chief halls: the hekal, or Holy, and the debir, or Holy of Holies. The New Testament calls it oikos, the house, and hieron, the enclosure. Solomon built it about 966 BC, and Nabuchodonozor destroyed it in 586 BC.

After the return from captivity, Zorobabel raised it again in 537 BC, so modestly that ancients who had seen the first wept. In the eighteenth year of his reign, 19 BC, Herod replaced it with a temple to equal or surpass Solomon's. Writers dispute whether three temples existed or only two, since Herod may have gradually replaced Zorobabel's work. The entry then details the courts, halls, and Herod's royal basilica, with its three naves and four rows of forty-one Corinthian columns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trustee-syste:
An account of the deputies the Church appoints to administer her property, technically called the "fabric" of the Church. In very early times ecclesiastical goods were split into three or four portions. The portion for upkeep took on the character of a juridical person, with laymen gradually called to share in its administration under the Church's approbation.

In England such officials were called churchwardens, generally two, one chosen by the priest and one by the parishioners, answerable to the bishop. The Council of Trent made an annual report obligatory. The Third Plenary Council of Baltimore set rules for American trustees, and a 1911 decree preferred the New York method of vesting title in a board.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veszprem:
Veszprém is a Hungarian diocese, suffragan to Esztergom, founded about 1009 by King St Stephen or perhaps by his wife Queen Gisela. The queen had the beautiful four-spired cathedral built, later destroyed by fire in 1276, gave rich gifts of gold and silver plate. Chose Veszprém as her burial place, an example followed by later Hungarian queens.

From the earliest times its bishop held the right of crowning the queen and served ex officio as her chancellor. Among Hungary's richest bishoprics in the fourteenth century, it boasted a celebrated school of theology and law. Demolished with cathedral and library when the town was destroyed in 1276 in wars between rival lords. After Mohács in 1526 the Turks ravaged the see's possessions, the Reformation shook its religious life, and Turkish wars ruined it further despite the efforts of bishops Forgách, Lippay, Szelepchényi, and Széchényi.
doe-osti-17135109-computational-fluid-dy:
Yeongshin Jeong, Tyler Sumner, and Matthew Weathered of Argonne use computer models to sharpen what a thermal hydraulics test rig can tell them, in a fiscal 2026 report. The THETA test article measures heat and flow behavior for reactor studies. Raw readings mean more when a flow simulation and a system code model help interpret them.

One part designs a flow conditioner for the rig and checks it with computational fluid dynamics. Smoother, known flow at the test section makes later data cleaner. The other part builds and updates a SAS system code model of THETA, reflecting fiscal 2026 changes to the rig. Conclusions tie the two models together as a standing aid for reading future experiments.
doe-osti-2574624-blueprinting-electrifie:
Final technical report DE-SC0025006, from Optimized Kinetics LLC under Noah Horesh with Colorado State University as partner, covers July 2024 to July 2025. Transit agencies electrifying bus fleets face a planning puzzle: which buses, which chargers, where, and at what cost. This SBIR project built an optimization framework that models a whole transit system and searches for the cheapest workable configuration.

The framework was demonstrated on a real transit system in Southern California. Against conventional planning, it cut infrastructure investment by up to 79 percent and total electrification cost by 25 percent. It named charging sites and specifications, bus deployment plans, and energy management settings. Inputs are standardized so the method can repeat in other regions, and the same machinery extends to delivery fleets. The report frames the work as a step toward a market-ready planning platform for agencies working with limited capital.
doe-osti-2575560-lamp-project-facility-a:
Planning document LA-UR-25-28296, also numbered LAMP-PM-PLAN-0005, by Robert Garnett of Los Alamos and issued August 11, 2025, counts the rooms the LAMP accelerator upgrade will need. Big projects fail quietly when workspace runs out. The plan tallies office, storage, and laboratory space across the project's life, from design and technology maturation through component testing to final removal and installation.

Peak demand passes 40,000 square feet, with an average near 25,000 across the schedule. Each space is color-coded by how hard it will be to get. Green means space already allocated to LAMP. Yellow marks space expected to transfer easily, and red flags shared space needing high-level negotiation. Tables break the need down by calendar year and type. A conceptual layout of the front-end upgrade anchors the discussion, and the technology maturation phase, fiscal 2024 to 2026, gets its own requirements section.
doe-osti-2586542-recovery-and-refining-o:
Daniel Laudal directed this final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-FE0032295, with Nolan Theaker of the University of North Dakota as principal investigator. Ahmed Essam and a long list of partners, from Barr Engineering to North American Coal, share the work. The project ran from August 2023 through April 2025 and studied recovering rare earth elements from lignite mine wastes in North Dakota.

Rare earths are vital for magnets and electronics, and coal wastes offer a domestic source. The report centers on a front-end engineering design study and cost estimate for the recovery and refining chain. It sizes concentrate facilities at Underwood and Center, listing the mining gear, loaders, haul trucks, and surface miners the plan would need. Risk mitigation and a path to commercialization close the study, with vendor quotes for major equipment gathered in an appendix.

doe-osti-3005970-multifunctional-catalys:
University of Virginia chemist Robert Davis reports under DOE award DE-FG02-95ER14549 on multifunctional catalysts that run tandem reactions of oxygenates. One target reaction turns carboxylic acids from biomass into alcohols. The catalyst pairs metal particles with metal oxide particles, and the design leans on hydrogen spillover between them. Supported tungsten oxide clusters reduce these acids well, but only after a late transition metal such as palladium is added as a promoter.

Work under the award probed what the active catalyst state is and how the reaction runs. One journal paper studied how domain size and support choice change the reducibility of tungsten oxide clusters on silica and titania. Two dissertations came out of the project, one on supported metal oxide catalysts for oxygenate conversion and one on size effects in carbides and oxides. The file pairs a DOE title page with the abstract and product list.
doe-osti-3012631-high-efficiency-and-tra:
Eaton Corporation's final technical report, submitted August 29, 2025, covers a project led by chief engineer James McCarthy Jr. with Ballard Power Systems and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The project, which ran from September 2022 to June 2025 under award DE-EE0009618, attacked the air handling system of hydrogen fuel cell trucks. That system is the largest parasitic power draw in a fuel cell vehicle and a common source of failures.

Eaton mechanically coupled its Twin Vortices compressor to a matching expander so exhaust energy helps drive the air supply, and added liquid spray humidification. The optimized heat exchanger design proved too costly to build as a prototype, so the team tested an off-the-shelf 34-liter unit instead. The work targets efficient, durable air systems for long-haul fuel cell trucks.
doe-osti-3017164-igiugig-comprehensive-e:
Becki Meadows, Kumaraguru Prabakar, and Yaswanth Nag Velaga of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this February 2026 report, NLR/TP-5700-92527. It gives implementation help for the comprehensive energy plan of Igiugig, a small community served by diesel generators. The report walks through the community's energy landscape and its energy journey so far, then turns the 2022 plan into buildable options.

Scenario tables compare system mixes unit by unit. The base case keeps two 65-kilowatt diesel units. Other cases add RivGen river-current turbines of 40 kilowatts, 253 kilowatt-hours of battery storage, and solar arrays of 125 or 200 kilowatts. The largest case adds a 100-kilowatt wind turbine as well. Each mix carries a system levelized cost, so the community can see what cleaner power would actually cost per unit of energy. Remote communities weighing diesel alternatives get a concrete template.
doe-osti-3017511-quantum-wrapper-network:
S J Ben Yoo of the University of California, Davis, led this final report for award DE-SC0022336, dated December 15, 2025, with Prem Kumar and Gregory Kanter also named on the record. The reporting period ran from June 2023 to February 2025. The project built quantum wrapper networking, a way to manage entanglement across optical networks that carry classical and quantum traffic together.

In this design, the quantum payload travels wrapped in a classical header of ordinary bits. Those bits steer the qubits end to end through a transparent optical network. Experiments measured what coexistence costs: with a classical transmitter enabled, quantum channel visibility fell to 31.9 percent before accidental counts were subtracted. Bit error rates and fringe offsets are reported in detail. The long goal is a global quantum internet. This project shows one workable traffic system for it, and prices the noise that classical channels add.
doe-osti-3022138-fy24-status-of-engineer:
Sandia report SAND2026-17777R, led by Edward Matteo, gives the fiscal year 2024 status of engineered barrier systems research for spent fuel and high-level waste disposal. Contributors came from Lawrence Berkeley and Los Alamos national laboratories and Vanderbilt University. The program studies the bentonite buffers, backfills, and seals that would surround waste packages in a geologic repository, and how heat, water, and chemistry change them over time.

Work summarized here spans laboratory experiments on bentonite behavior, materials characterization, and coupled process modeling. One thread follows the international HotBENT heated-bentonite experiment, where the modeling teams plan a path from two-dimensional thermal-hydrologic models toward full three-dimensional coupled models checked against experimental data. The report is a program-wide snapshot rather than a single study, cataloguing progress task by task.
doe-osti-3022415-arcticshark-uncrewed-ae:
A Department of Energy fact sheet profiles the ArcticShark, an uncrewed aerial system run by the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement user facility. The aircraft flies small-scale, precise, repeatable patterns over areas of scientific interest, including the ARM ground observatories in Alabama and Oklahoma, filling the gap between tower measurements and crewed research flights.

Its printed specifications give a 22-foot wingspan, a maximum gross weight of 650 pounds, and a 100-pound payload capacity. Flights typically run five to eight hours at a cruise speed near 60 miles per hour, between 500 feet above ground and about 15,000 feet above sea level. Instruments measure aerosols, atmospheric gases and water vapor, infrared temperature, and multispectral imagery for surface and cloud studies. Data pass quality checks by ARM staff and are released free through the ARM Data Center.

expressive-voice-culture-including-the-e:
Southwick's Expressive Voice Culture sets out the Emerson System of voice training. Jessie Eldridge Southwick taught voice culture at the Emerson College of Oratory. Her preface states the system's core idea in plain terms. The voice is a natural reporter of the person who speaks.

Tone and movement should express thought and feeling without self-consciousness. The treatise joins technique to expression rather than drilling sound alone. Chapter I lays out principles of voice culture for the beginner. True culture shows in exact modulation that matches inner purpose. Southwick offers her book as one contribution to a broad subject. Teachers of elocution and public speakers form its natural audience.
fair-em: Fair Em, a comedy presented as Shakespeare's work and marked apocryphal, centres on Em, the miller's daughter of Manchester. William the Conqueror, smitten by her portrait, pursues her while Danish and English nobles scheme around him. Blanch of Denmark, Mariana of Sweden and the miller's household complete a tangle of disguise, rivalry and love that ends, as comedy requires, in sorting out.
fanny-and-the-servant-problem:
Jerome K. Jerome published this four-act comedy in 1909 and billed it as a quite possible play. The character list gives the joke away. Fanny, now Lady Bantock and wife of Vernon Wetherell, keeps a butler, a housekeeper, a maid, a second footman, and a still-room maid, and every one of them is named Bennet.

The Bennets are Fanny's own family, placed through the house by their daughter the mistress. Her aunts by marriage, the formidable Misses Wetherell, regard the staff as fixtures of the family and know nothing of the connection. Fanny's old music-hall companions turn up as well, billed as Our Empire in the programme. The comedy runs on near-discovery: a household where mistress and servants are one family pretending at the forms.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_climate-:
Senior officials in President Richard Nixon's administration were debating climate change as early as 1969. This briefing book from the Archive's Climate Change Transparency Project was posted in April 2024. Rachel Santarsiero edited it, drawing on declassified documents.

Inside Nixon's inner circle, officials weighed rising carbon dioxide, sea-level rise, and extreme temperatures. They also argued over fossil-fuel use, the source of the problem. The records surprise many readers, because they show the basic science and policy choices were understood at the top of government more than fifty years ago. Later administrations inherited a problem their predecessors had already named.
homes-and-how-to-make-them:
E C Gardner, an architect, wrote these letters on home building, issued at Boston in 1875. The book is cast as letters between the architect and his friends. Gardner's preface states the aim: practical hints for those about to build. He hopes to feed a growing demand for better and truer work.

Bay-windows earn a full, balanced hearing in one letter. A good one can cheer a graceless room, Gardner allows. Yet plain large windows often beat a fussy bay, he warns. False and useless features draw his cordial hatred throughout. Home builders of the time got taste and thrift taught in a friendly voice.
jerusalem:
Selma Lagerlof wrote Jerusalem, a novel from the Swedish, translated by Velma Swanston Howard. Book one follows the Ingmarssons, a farming family in Dalarna. A young farmer plows one summer morning, happy at the thought of sowing his rye. Sunshine and fair weather make him feel a child of Heaven, he wonders.

Hellgum, a preacher returned from America, brings a new way in book two. Karin likes his teaching for its works and service over mere feeling, Lagerlof writes. He claims he can heal any who have faith in him. An auction, a departure of pilgrims, and Zion fill the later books.
john-marshall-and-the-constitution-a-chr:
John Marshall and the Constitution is Edward S. Corwin's chronicle of the Supreme Court under its great chief justice. It appeared in 1920 as volume sixteen of the Chronicles of America series, from Yale University Press. Nine chapters run from the establishment of the national judiciary to an epilogue. A bibliographical note and index close the volume.

Corwin treats Marshall's early years, then Jefferson's war on the judiciary and the trial of Aaron Burr. Later chapters set out Marshall's tenets of nationalism and the sanctity of contracts. The menace of state rights and a portrait among friends and neighbors follow. The book explains how one judge's rulings built the federal court's lasting power.
lessons-in-life-for-all-who-will-read-th:
T. S. Arthur published Lessons in Life, for All Who Will Read Them, at Philadelphia in 1851. His preface opens with a truism: we are never too old to learn. He asks readers not to let repetition dull that truth.

At every stage of life, Arthur says, we remain learners. Human life lies open like a great book before us. Studying its lessons well should make us wiser and happier. Arthur wrote many temperance and domestic tales for popular readers. This volume gathers his moral teaching in short, plain chapters. Arthur edited popular story papers for family reading. His lessons favor home, work, and temperance virtues.
liberalism-and-the-social-problem:
Winston Churchill published Liberalism and the Social Problem as a young statesman. The book gathers his case for Liberal reform in Edwardian Britain. Its title joins a political creed to the era's great question.

Poverty amid plenty defined that social problem for his generation. Churchill argues that Liberal policy must answer it directly. Speeches on reform, labor, and the state fill the volume. Readers meet a future war leader as a rising reformer. His bold prose style already shows its famous energy here. His free trade speeches made headlines in those years. Churchill broke with the Conservatives over such questions earlier.
manual-of-ship-subsidies-an-historical-s:
The Manual of Ship Subsidies sums up the subsidy systems of all nations. Edwin M. Bacon wrote it, and the title page dates it 1911. His first chapter defines a subsidy as a government grant in aid of trade. Different countries, he shows, shade the meaning differently.

Subsidies came as building premiums, navigation bounties, and fishing bounties. Postal pay for ocean mails and naval subventions were other forms. Britain, Bacon notes, used chiefly postal subsidies and naval subventions. Those payments bought ships built to Admiralty rules for war use. The manual served the great shipping debates of its day. It remains a clear record of how states nursed their merchant fleets.
nasa-tm-19650021022-space-vehicle-sa-6-t:
Marshall's Telemetry Performance Evaluation Office issued this June 23, 1965, report on the SA-6 Saturn vehicle. SA-6 was a Saturn I test flight. Its telemetry system radioed measurements back during flight. Ten links in all carried the data, six in the first stage and four in the instrument unit and upper stage.

Evaluators review the full system as flown, link by link. Telemetry is the only witness to much of a test flight. If a link fails, that part of the flight goes unrecorded. A formal evaluation tells the next team which links held up, and which parts of the system needed attention.
nasa-tm-19650022946-telemetry-computer-i:
Donald E Jamison prepared this July 1965 report at Goddard on joining computers directly to telemetry work. Telemetry signals pour in from spacecraft at high speed. They must be reduced and converted before anyone can use them. Jamison's system links a high-speed digital computer with that signal reduction and conversion work, in the Data Systems Division.

Joining the steps saves hand work and shortens delays. Data can be checked while a pass is still fresh in mind. The report comes from Goddard's data processing branch, which handled many missions. It shows data handling becoming a computer task, rather than a room full of separate machines and paper.
nasa-tm-19660018739-apollo-unified-s-ban:
K E Peltzer, in Goddard's Manned Flight Support Office, described the Apollo Unified S-Band system in April 1966. One radio system would carry all traffic between Apollo spacecraft and ground stations. Voice, telemetry, ranging, and television all share that single unified link. Putting every signal on one system saved weight and antennas on the spacecraft.

Reliability was the deeper reason for the design. A single, well-tested link could be backed up and monitored as one unit. Ground stations around the world used the same standard. Peltzer's system description gave all teams one reference. Apollo's crews spoke to Earth through this system on every flight to the Moon.
nasa-tm-19670002037-simulation-of-an-opt:
Charles R. Newman and Manuel Lerman, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this March 1966 paper on spacecraft pointing. An optical aspect system tells a spinning spacecraft which way it is facing. Their work simulates such a system before any hardware flies.

The authors describe a method to calculate one key angle. It is the angle through which a telescope on the spinning craft sees the sunlit part of a central body. They treat that body as a sphere for the calculation. A good simulation lets engineers check the design's geometry on paper first.
nasa-tm-19670002051-an-interferometric-r:
Diane Marie Tillson wrote this report at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in September 1966. It lays out an interferometric ranging system, a way to measure distance with extreme precision. The catalog record notes that the system uses a continuous-wave laser as its light source.

The contents trace the full design, starting with a history of ranging methods and the theory of lasing and mode selection. A dual-mode gas laser feeds a Michelson interferometer, and a detection circuit watches the beat note signal between the modes. Tillson describes how signal strength and accuracy limits were analyzed. Measurement sections cover finding null points and reducing the data. A second, alternate high accuracy system is also described, with its own frequency stabilization method and results.
nasa-tm-19680018330-the-lunar-orbiter-ph:
G. Calvin Broome and Joseph C. Moorman of Langley Research Center describe the Lunar Orbiter photographic system in this May 1967 conference paper. Lunar Orbiters I, II, and III flew in 1966 and early 1967. Their main goal was photographing the Moon to help pick safe Apollo landing sites.

Secondary goals covered the Moon's origin, history, and gravitational field. The authors describe the full Orbiter system, stressing the photographic system's design and flight performance. They weigh the problems and advantages of film cameras for deep space work. Selected photographs and performance data from the first three missions are presented. The paper records how film imaging served lunar exploration.
nasa-tm-19680020501-nerva-xe-1-control-d:
David J. Robinson of Lewis Research Center reports low-temperature hydrogen tests of the NERVA XE-1 control drum actuator in this 1968 memorandum, TM X-52465. NERVA was a nuclear rocket engine, and rotating drums set its reactor power level. The actuator turns those drums and must keep working while breathing very cold hydrogen gas.

Earlier cold tests had used helium only, so Robinson's team ran the actuator on hydrogen across a deep cold range. Judged as part of a closed loop positioning system, it worked well in steady running through sudden drops in temperature. One warning stood out: an actuator locked in place through such a chill later behaved erratically after unlocking.
nasa-tm-19680020756-capache-payload-reco:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this service manual for the Capache payload recovery system in December 1967. Capache brings sounding rocket payloads back to Earth by parachute. It serves rockets of the Nike-Cajun and Nike-Apache class, as the report record states.

The manual describes each assembly in turn. Sections cover the parachute and its cylinder, the severance section with its shaped charge ring, and the forward adapter ring. The sequencer assembly gets detailed treatment, including power supply, electronic timer, barometric sensor, and radio beacon. A housing assembly and the full sequence of operation close the description section. Checkout and adjustment procedures follow for technicians who prepare the system.
nasa-tm-19680025278-requirements-for-spa:
Ward W. Wilcox and Robert H. Rollins of NASA's Office of Advanced Research and Technology set out requirements for space propulsion systems in this paper. Their scope covers thrusting devices used in and beyond Earth orbit. The time frame is roughly the next decade, depending more on funding than on technology.

The paper divides into three sections built on three questions. First, where must the system operate? The environments beyond Earth orbit shape every propulsion choice. Later sections follow from those operating conditions. Wilcox and Rollins write for planners deciding which propulsion systems deserve development. Their requirements frame future spacecraft propulsion work at NASA.
nasa-tm-19690008747-datadigit-system:
R. J. Stattel and J. W. Fennel Jr. describe the DataDigit system in this December 1968 Goddard preprint, numbered X-721-68-483. DataDigit formed part of a pulse-position-modulation telemetry system used widely on sounding rocket flights. Goddard's Sounding Rocket Instrumentation Section designed it to stamp time onto flight records in a form people could read at a glance.

Once each second, the system prints time as three plain numerals on analog paper records. Grid lines mark the start of every second as the paper runs. Its time source could be a countdown clock or the standard NASA time code. The authors stress the gain: printed digits are far easier to read than the usual rapid pulse code.
nasa-tm-19690029252-vhf-satellite-naviga:
Goddard Space Flight Center issued this January 1968 report, numbered X-733-68-30, proposing a VHF satellite navigation experiment. Growing air traffic over the North Atlantic drove the search for better position finding. The experiment would range to the ATS-1 and ATS-3 satellites, already in geosynchronous orbit, using very high frequency radio signals.

Finding how accurate such ranging could be, with stated confidence levels, is the primary goal. A secondary goal is proving aircraft positions can be fixed in real time under flight conditions. The sidetone ranging method needs far less satellite bandwidth than rival schemes, the authors note. Sections describe the ground control center, a reference terminal, and the aircraft terminal in turn.
nasa-tm-19700015498-computerized-microst:
J. W. Lyons and three co-workers at the Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, wrote this report in April 1970. It describes a computerized system for measuring very small strains in test materials. The system can sense changes at the scale of a microinch.

A capacitance bridge takes the readings on its own, linked to a computer. The setup measures lasting bends, loop areas from loading cycles, and total strain energy. Tests use the normal load-and-release pull method. The report also covers how the system was simulated, calibrated, and where its errors can arise.
nasa-tm-19700026504-manned-lunar-landing:
The Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this Apollo internal note, number 67-EG-16. It sets out a strategy for system management and operations in crewed lunar landing work. Landing on the Moon took thousands of people working in step across many teams, plus a spacecraft system unlike any flown before.

Its argument is that mission planning must build an operating strategy alongside the hardware itself, not after it. Test flights would exercise the lunar module, yet the real landing approach would still be its first true use. A simple theoretical landing path is sketched, then set aside as impossible, since it would demand endless engine power. The practical strategy must instead fit a finite engine and the Moon's real surface conditions.
nasa-tm-19710004699-on-the-structure-of-:
NASA issued this study on the structure of multivariable systems. Such systems have many inputs and many outputs acting at once, as in a spacecraft steered by several controls. Control engineers need clear rules for how the parts of such a system hang together before they can design for it.

The paper's main purpose is to state and prove a structure theorem for systems that do not change with time. The systems are written with state, input, and output vectors linked by constant matrices. The theorem is meant for controller design and synthesis work. It is applied here to two standing problems, realization and decoupling, where separate control of separate outputs is the goal.
nasa-tm-19710011824-development-of-low-c:
Edward F Miller of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 symposium in Genoa, Italy, on satellite communications. It presents NASA work on cheap ground receivers for television sent from synchronous satellites. Such satellites hang over one spot on the equator. The goal was television service that ordinary viewers could afford.

The systems described pick up microwave signals from orbit. They then shift the carrier frequency and change the signal format. The result feeds ordinary VHF and UHF television sets without costly gear. Miller placed the work among studies by other nations and groups. Cheap receivers were the missing link for direct satellite broadcasting.
on-books-and-the-housing-of-them:
William Ewart Gladstone wrote this essay on books and libraries. Gladstone was Britain's great statesman and a famed book collector. He worries that books will soon crowd available space. He compares the book population with the human population. A book, he says, has a body and a soul.

Gladstone warns against rich bindings on poor printing. Renaissance makers matched fine covers with fine pages, he notes. Cheap books should still show fitness and care, he argues. The essay gives rules for housing a large library. It remains a guide for serious collectors.
pearl-maiden-a-tale-of-the-fall-of-jerus: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Pearl-Maiden, the contents and dedication, with no chapter text visible. The title page names H. Rider Haggard and calls the book a tale of the fall of Jerusalem, first published in 1901. The contents follow a heroine named Miriam, born in a prison at Caesarea, kept by the Essenes as their queen. She is swept into the Roman war, the Sanhedrim, the triumph of the Caesars, and the judgment of Domitian.
philip-gilbert-hamerton-an-autobiography:
Philip Gilbert Hamerton began an autobiography meant for publication after his death, but sudden death stopped it at his twenty-fourth year. His wife Eugénie explains in her preface that the fragment seemed too brief alone. Since his written life ends exactly at their marriage, she could continue it from intimate knowledge, and friends encouraged her to try, though English was foreign to her.

The result joins his Autobiography, 1834 to 1858, with her Memoir, 1858 to 1894. Letters from Robert Louis Stevenson and Robert Browning appear by permission. Hamerton, the art critic of The Intellectual Life, is shown whole: artist, etcher, and husband.
pocahontas-a-poem:
Virginia Carter Castleman wrote Pocahontas, a long narrative poem about the Powhatan princess whose name became part of American legend. Castleman dedicates the work to Virginia, her mother state, and shapes the poem as a tribute laid at its feet. The poem retells the famous story in verse, from childhood among the marshes to the journey across the ocean.

Eight parts carry the arc: the little princess, the wizard, the arrival of Smith and Newport. The coronation of Powhatan, a guardian angel section, the parting, the marriage to John Rolfe, and the final London scenes. Pocahontas appears as Matoax, dearest daughter of the mighty chief Powhatan, in scenes drawn from the standard colonial accounts. Readers get a romantic, period version of the legend, written in the admiring voice of its era.
podcast-joerogan-u04t4fkBIeM:
Security expert Gavin de Becker talks safety with Joe Rogan in episode 2411 of the Joe Rogan Experience. De Becker wrote The Gift of Fear, the bestseller that taught readers to trust their instincts. His firm protects famous and powerful people from stalkers and attackers.

De Becker explains the warning signs that come before violence, from forced friendliness to refusing to hear no. He argues that fear, read right, is a survival tool rather than a weakness. Rogan asks about stalkers, public attacks, and staying calm under threat. Listeners leave with a sharper eye for danger in daily life.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Rvaxb-xHREM:
A globalist agenda to destroy the family is the charge at the center of this Tucker Carlson episode. Carlson argues that powerful institutions push policies that weaken marriage, lower birth rates, and separate children from parents. He presents the pattern as a plan, not a series of accidents.

The episode works through the policies and cultural shifts Carlson blames, from education to public health. He then turns to escape: how families can protect their own lives against the pressure. Stories and examples carry the warning more than charts. Alarmed and watchful viewers get the host's darkest charge yet, with his way out.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Xg9rKJGlieM:
A top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was framed for Pentagon leaks, Tucker Carlson reports in this episode. The adviser was removed amid a leak hunt that Carlson says was really about Iran policy. The episode presents the affair as a setup by war hawks inside the building.

Carlson lays out the timeline of the accusations and the adviser's removal. He argues the real fight was over whether America would strike Iran. The guest's side of the story gets a full hearing against the official line. Wary and watching viewers see how Washington knife fights hide inside leak stories.
poetical-works-of-johnson-parnell-gray-a:
Four Augustan poets share this Edinburgh volume of 1855: Samuel Johnson, Thomas Parnell, Thomas Gray. Tobias Smollett, presented with memoirs, critical dissertations, and explanatory notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan. Johnson's section leads, with his life followed by London, his Juvenal imitation of 1738, and the Vanity of Human Wishes. The other great imitation, poems in which a young, poor Johnson surveyed the city and mankind with majestic pessimism.

Prologues spoken by Garrick, odes on the seasons, and miscellaneous pieces complete Johnson's share before the volume moves to his companions. Parnell the hermit's poet, Gray of the Elegy, and Smollett the novelist in verse. Gilfillan's series put the eighteenth-century canon, edited and judged, into cheap Victorian hands. The grouping itself is an argument: these four, for the editor, are the century's second rank made permanent, the necessary company around its giants.
polly-oliver-s-problem:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published Polly Oliver's Problem in Boston with Houghton, Mifflin in 1896, in an edition fronted by her portrait and a biographical sketch. The sketch tells her story: born Kate Douglas Smith in Philadelphia, raised partly in Hollis, Maine, seasoned in California. Writing at Quillcote, her colonial summer house among the Saco River hills, the New England neighborhood that feeds her fiction.

Polly Oliver is one of Wiggin's spirited heroines, a girl with a problem to solve by work and wit rather than by waiting. Wiggin, who also created Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, wrote about girls and rural communities with humor and respect, drawing her scenes from the Maine villages she knew. The biographical front matter makes this edition a double portrait: the author in her landscape, and the heroine she built from it, in one small, handsome volume.
the-backwoods-of-canada-being-letters-fr:
Letters from the wife of an emigrant officer, printed in London in 1836 by Charles Knight, describe home life in British America. The volume belongs to a series called the Library of Entertaining Knowledge, issued under a society for spreading useful knowledge. The writer is named in brackets as Catharine Parr Traill.

A contents list begins with amusements and a captain's goldfinch, suggesting daily detail rather than grand events. Traill's letters aim to show the domestic economy of settler life, meaning food, housing, work, and costs in the backwoods. For British readers thinking of emigrating, such plain home facts had clear practical value.
the-banks-of-wye-a-poem:
Robert Bloomfield, author of The Farmer's Boy, published a poem in four books in London in 1811. He calls the work a journal and dedicates it to friends in Gloucestershire, recalling past pleasures with them. A picture shows the Wye seen through a gateway at Crickhowell.

In a preface Bloomfield explains that, in the summer of 1807, friends planned a short trip down the Wye and through part of South Wales. Lines he had written on Shooter's Hill during ill health caught their notice. They invited him to join them, and the verses that follow grew out of that journey and their kindness.
the-columbiad-a-poem:
Joel Barlow wrote this patriotic poem on Columbus and America, with an Italian motto from Gierus and a preface dated 1809. In that preface Barlow explains his design and its difficulties. A classical reader, he says, will see the obstacles in fitting his subject to a poetical manner with real dignity and usefulness.

The Columbiad, he states, is a patriotic poem, and its subject is national and historical. That alone should interest his countrymen. Yet most of its events were recent, important, and well known, which made them inflexible to the hand of fiction. The poem therefore could not properly follow the regular epic form of more splendid works of the kind. Barlow thus warns readers to expect a national poem shaped by fact rather than by invented adventure, a defense of his method placed before the verse itself.
the-farmer-s-boy-a-rural-poem:
Robert Bloomfield wrote The Farmer's Boy, a rural poem in four parts for the four seasons, and this third edition was printed at London in 1800. A sonnet in praise of the young poet stands at the front.

Bloomfield was a farm lad himself, and the poem follows a boy's work through the year: ploughing, sowing, hay time, and harvest. The sonnet calls his lyre sweet and true to each charm of country life. Plain speech and close watching of field tasks won the poem a wide fame, and it made a working man's verse a best seller of its day.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: Rossiter Johnson was supervising editor of The Great Events by Famous Historians. Charles F. Horne and John Rudd were literary editors. Walter F. Austin was directing editor. This record is Volume V. Only front matter is present here: the title page and the start of a contents list. The contents open with an outline narrative by Horne. The first subject named is feudalism, under its Frankish birth and English development. No further pieces are named.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
The issue dated November 4, 1897 is No. 52 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead items concern Cuba. The situation there remains much the same. The week's noteworthy event is a sad shipwreck, on October 16. A Spanish steamer wrecked on the coast of Pinar del Rio, bound from Havana to Bahia Honda.

The steamer, the Triton, carried soldiers' ammunition, money, and mules for use against the Cubans. She was so heavily laden that her decks stood only a few feet above the water. Sailors on the dock feared she could not weather a storm. Near her destination she ran aground. She was too deep in the water to pass a bank she ordinarily cleared. When she grounded, the waves washed over her decks and the mules panicked.
the-negro-problem:
The Negro Problem gathers seven essays by leading Black writers of its day, and its contents page gives each a page number. Booker T. Washington opens with Industrial Education for the Negro at page 7. W. E. Burghardt DuBois follows with The Talented Tenth, Charles W. Chesnutt with The Disfranchisement of the Negro, and Wilford H. Smith with The Negro and the Law.

H. T. Kealing writes on the characteristics of the Negro people, Paul Laurence Dunbar on representative American Negroes, and T. Thomas Fortune on the Negro's place in American life. Washington's essay is prefaced by a printed summary of its argument. The race must learn the difference between being worked and working, it says. Teaching the present generation to work and save will create wealth. From that wealth alone can come leisure, and the chance of higher education.
the-new-jerusalem:
G. K. Chesterton's The New Jerusalem lays out a journey in thirteen chapters plus a conclusion, listed in its contents. The Way of the Cities and The Way of the Desert lead to The Gates of the City. Chapters on the philosophy of sight-seeing, the streets and groups of the city, the battle with the dragon, the meaning of the Crusade, and the problem of Zionism follow.

Chapter I opens at Christmas. Chesterton leaves his little garden among beech fields lying between the Thames and the Chilterns, to walk backwards through history toward the place Christmas came from. A traveller who has lost his way, he says, must return to a sign-post, and modern man has forgotten even the name of his destination.
un-un-res-first-report-of-the-secretary-:
Legal ground rules for the first United Nations Emergency Force in Egypt are set out in this 1956 report of the Secretary-General, document A/3526. The force had been rushed to Egypt during the Suez Crisis to stand between Egyptian and invading troops. No UN force quite like it had existed before, so its legal status had to be built from scratch.

The report covers the force's rights, duties, and immunities on Egyptian soil. It explains how troops would be supplied, disciplined, and protected under law. The arrangements became a template for peacekeeping forces sent around the world afterward.
victor-roy-a-masonic-poem:
Harriett Annie Wilkins wrote Victor Roy, a Masonic poem, and dedicated it by permission to Daniel Spry, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Canada. Her preface says the poem grew from an anecdote printed in The Craftsman. She makes no grand claims for it: not a story of great depth, she writes, and not an attempt to soar to Alpine heights or dig up hidden treasures of thought.

Her tale is a simple one, told in simple words, about lives like those around us. It tells of sorrows borne daily by suffering people, and of the faith that lets them endure by seeing Him who is invisible. Cross-bearers, she hopes, become crown-wearers in the end. She praises the Masonic order, too, as an ancient body marked by its Grand Master Builder and calm in its wide charity.
yeast-a-problem:
No author's name is printed in the pages present here for this novel. Chapter one, on the philosophy of fox-hunting, opens at a hunt meet. Some forty red coats gather by a thorn-topped ditch and a broken gate. Young farmers, horse dealers, a surgeon, and schoolboys fill the field. Lancelot Smith, aged twenty-three, rides forward with two good horses and nothing else to do.

The narrator mocks linking a soul's state to the weather. Lancelot once kept a soul-almanack mixing barometer readings with virtue. A shilling given to a tramp, later found drunk, punctures the system. Social satire and a young man's education drive the tale.
